$comment: Snapshot for /math: per-family review notes (explainer, caveats, lean detail, pages) and openai/math's manuscript map (summary, papers) at `commit`. Written by scripts/build-math-reels-data.mts --import; the review grades themselves live in components/articles/openai-math/catalogue-data.ts.

100.explainer: Bang's plank theorem says strips covering a convex body must have total width at least the body's minimum width; the 3-D cylinder analogue conjectured that cylinders covering a body need total cross-section at least half the smallest shadow, with a regular tetrahedron covered by two cylinders as the equality case. Tilting the two cylinder directions into many slightly different nearby directions, with triangular cross-sections, saves a second-order amount of area, so the 1/2 bound is false.
100.caveats: The saving is tiny ((13/6000)eps^2 to leading order, about 5e-10 of the normalized area at the largest allowed eps=1/2000, using 2*ceil(2/eps^2)=16,000,000 cylinders) and the number of cylinders grows like 1/eps^2; it refutes the 1/2 constant but leaves the true constant between 1/3 (Bezdek-Litvak) and just below 1/2 open. Four manuscripts for one counterexample; the 'every nondegenerate tetrahedron' extension is by an affine-invariance remark not formalized. No public expert reaction found.
100.lean: main theorem formalized — ComparatorChallenges/TriangularCovering.lean (A_min = sqrt2, the asymptotic 1/2-(13/6000)eps^2+O(eps^4), and the strict counterexample) and the aggregate CylinderCovering.lean (four-paper main incl.
100.summary: Covers the entire closed regular tetrahedron by finitely many cylinders with compact triangular perpendicular bases whose total area is less than half its smallest orthogonal projection area. This disproves Bang's half-area cylinder-covering bound and the stronger directionwise normalized conjecture in dimension three.

papers.title: Finite angular cylinder covers below the half-area bound
Finite cylinder approximation of ruled sets
Slope-field perturbations of the two-cylinder covering
Finite triangular approximation of radial sweeps

101.explainer: The isotropic constant measures how much volume a convex body has relative to its spread; Bourgain asked if it is bounded (yes, Klartag-Lehec 2024), and the sharper conjecture says simplices are the worst case in every dimension. By Fradelizi-Marin Sola this is equivalent to a sharp entropy inequality: among log-concave distributions with given covariance, products of one-sided exponentials have least entropy. The proof transports a Gaussian onto the density, reparametrizes the Jacobian with the scalar Gaussian-to-exponential transport, and controls the entropy deficit through a Gaussian chaos decomposition where degree >=2 parts give a spectral gap.
101.caveats: Unformalized and not peer-reviewed, 42 pages of hard analysis (Brenier/Caffarelli transport, matrix-valued Ornstein-Uhlenbeck/chaos decomposition, rational-constant scalar inequalities verified by polynomial bounds plus tail estimates, approximation for equality cases); treat as a claim. If correct it is bigger than the summary states, since it would also settle the nonsymmetric Mahler conjecture (the symmetric Mahler conjecture for the cube is not addressed).
101.lean: none — no lean/docs/101.md, no entry in lean/formalization.yaml, no Comparator challenge for the entropy or simplex inequality.
101.summary: Proves that simplices uniquely maximize the isotropic constant among convex bodies in every dimension, resolving the strong isotropic constant conjecture. Also establishes the sharp entropy lower bound for log-concave probability densities, with equality precisely for invertible affine images of products of one-sided exponential laws.

papers.title: A sharp entropy bound and the simplex inequality for isotropic constants

102.explainer: Unique Games asks you to label vertices so that each edge's permutation constraint holds; the conjecture says telling 99%-satisfiable from 1%-satisfiable instances is NP-hard. If true (as claimed here), the simple SDP-rounding algorithms engineers already use (Goemans-Williamson for Max-Cut at 0.878, the 2-approximation for Vertex Cover, Raghavendra's basic SDP for any CSP) are the best any polynomial-time algorithm can do unless P=NP. The proof's key trick is a 'latent noise' gadget: a nonlinear map C on a larger binary space V that honest labelings evaluate stably under a hidden perturbation (fixing the 1/2-completeness loss of the earlier 2-to-2 rank-one test), while any family of high-rank linear observations still detects the perturbation, so the Khot-Minzer-Safra inverse shortcode theorem still applies for soundness.
102.caveats: The proof imports external theorems as black boxes in the paper (Khot-Minzer-Safra Grassmann expansion via the Barak-Kothari-Steurer inverse shortcode theorem, Hastad's parity hardness, Dinur-Steurer parallel repetition); the Lean development must contain these or equivalents since it uses no extra axioms, which is itself a remarkable claim I could not build or inspect in full.
102.lean: main theorem formalized: Comparator challenges UniqueGamesTheorem.lean (OAI.UniqueGamesTheorem.theorem11), OptimalMaxCut.lean, VertexCover.lean, MinUncut.lean, DirectedFeedback.lean; permitted axioms only propext/Quot.sound/Classical.choice; no sorry or custom axiom anywhere in the OAI library (checked by grep).
102.summary: Proves Khot's Unique Games Conjecture. Independent direct reductions also establish NP-hardness, on unweighted graphs, of approximation beyond the Goemans–Williamson ratio for Max-Cut, below factor two for Vertex Cover, and within any fixed constant factor for Min-UnCut and directed feedback vertex set. These direct proofs use established PCP and Label Cover hardness results.

papers.title: The Unique Games Theorem
A Direct Proof of Optimal Max-Cut Hardness
The Factor-Two Hardness Threshold for Vertex Cover
Constant-factor hardness of Min-UnCut
Constant-factor hardness of directed feedback vertex set

103.explainer: BPL is what a computer with logarithmic memory can decide if it may flip coins (with small error); L is the same without coins. The claim is that coins never help small-memory computation, the space analogue of P=BPP, which theorists widely believed but could only approach to within a log^{1/2} factor in space for 25 years. The approach estimates the acceptance probability (I-S)^{-1}e of the configuration graph through a hierarchy of 'corrected' sparse transition matrices, evaluated by fingerprinted recursive calls whose total memory telescopes to O(log n); a median over all O(log n)-bit random environments, enumerated deterministically, gives the answer.
103.caveats: Single 108-page manuscript with no formalization, no reasoning trace and no companion. The proof uses property (T) mixing results of Shalom as an external input, fingerprinting/catalytic-style shared bit vectors and a delicate recursive space accounting; space-accounting errors are the classic failure mode for claimed log-space simulations, and nothing here is machine-checked. The polynomial time bound has unspecified (likely astronomically large) exponents. No public expert assessment of this specific result found as of 2026-10-07.
103.lean: none (lean/OAI/Computability/Logspace/Deterministic.lean contains only machine definitions and basic run lemmas, 585 lines, no main theorem and no Comparator challenge)
103.summary: Proves L=RL=BPL, resolving derandomization for bounded-error logarithmic-space computation. An effective compiler converts each randomized polynomial-time logarithmic-space machine deciding a language with one-sided or two-sided error into a deterministic logarithmic-space decider with explicit polynomial running-time bounds.

papers.title: Exact derandomization of logarithmic space: L = RL = BPL

104.explainer: Mean-payoff games model controller synthesis and verification: two players push a token round a weighted graph and fight over the long-run average weight. They sit in NP and coNP but nobody knew a fast algorithm when weights are written in binary. The claim brings them down to n^{O(log n)}-style time, the same status parity games reached in 2017, which matters to model-checking tools that reduce to these games.
104.caveats: Quasipolynomial, not polynomial; P membership remains open. Stochastic result covers expectation-of-liminf with threshold zero, not general value computation of simple stochastic games (Condon's problem) as far as the abstract states. Deterministic version is unformalized; only the randomized one is Lean-checked.
104.lean: partial formalization: RandomizedMeanPayoff.lean (randomized quasipolynomial algorithm, success 7/8) and TruffetCounterexample.lean; the deterministic, stochastic and parity-extension papers are not formalized
104.summary: Gives deterministic algorithms using 2^(O((log (L+2))²)) bit operations, for complete binary input length L, for ordinary mean-payoff games and two separate extensions. They compute exact values and optimal positional strategies in ordinary games, the nonnegative expectation-of-liminf value set in turn-based stochastic games, and the winning set for nonnegative liminf mean payoff conjoined with parity. Signed rewards, rational chance probabilities, and parity priorities are unrestricted and binary-encoded.

papers.title: Turn-Based Stochastic Mean-Payoff Games in Deterministic Quasipolynomial Time
Mean-payoff parity games in quasipolynomial time
Deterministic quasipolynomial-time mean-payoff games
Randomized quasipolynomial-time mean-payoff games

105.explainer: Unique Games insists each label has exactly one valid reply; 2-to-1 games allow two. Hardness with perfect completeness (the YES instances are fully satisfiable) is what coloring-style reductions need, because a 3-colourable graph has no 'almost' about it. This is the strongest of Khot's d-to-1 conjectures and feeds directly into family 106.
105.caveats: The paper's own external inputs are Grassmann expansion (KMS), parallel repetition and a perfect-completeness PCP; it credits a 'close counterpart' of its bilinear-form step in Fei-Minzer-Wang Lemmas 5.15-5.16. 2-to-1 is stronger than 4-to-1, so this genuinely extends FMW, but the novelty margin over a nine-day-old human result is smaller than the summary suggests. No public expert assessment of this specific result found as of 2026-10-07.
105.lean: main theorem formalized: PerfectCompleteness.lean (OAI.PerfectCompleteness.Theorem11.exists_reduction), ~137k lines, standard axioms only
105.summary: Proves Khot's 2-to-1 Games Conjecture with perfect completeness: for every fixed rational δ ∈ (0,1), it is NP-hard to distinguish satisfiable games from games whose optimum is at most δ, on explicit unweighted instances. The alphabet depends only on δ, and every right-hand label has exactly two preimages under each constraint map.

papers.title: Perfect completeness for 2-to-1 games

106.explainer: Given a graph you know is 3-colorable, can you efficiently color it with 4, 10 or 1000 colors? Best algorithms need about n^0.2 colors, and for 25 years the hardness side was stuck at 5. This paper (and Fei-Minzer-Wang days earlier) says any constant number is NP-hard, and even finding an independent set of a delta fraction is hard. The construction gives every vertex a phase on a circle; satisfying assignments keep phases consistent across projection links, edges force phases about half a turn apart, and three arcs of the circle give a proper 3-coloring.
106.caveats: The family title and summary ('It is NP-hard to color a three-colorable graph using any fixed number c>=3 of colors') present as new a corollary that Fei-Minzer-Wang already published on 14 Sep 2026; the paper itself credits them correctly. What is new is three-colorability of the whole graph combined with arbitrarily small independence ratio, proved directly from ordinary Label Cover (not via 105). Proof uses Austin's continuous junta theorem and a Ramsey-type alignment lemma, so constants are enormous.
106.lean: main theorem formalized: IndependentSets.lean (OAI.LargeIndependentSets.mainTheoremReal), ~94k lines in OAI/Combinatorics/IndependentSets, standard axioms
106.summary: It is NP-hard to color a three-colorable graph using any fixed number c ≥ 3 of colors. More strongly, for every fixed 0 < δ < 1/3, a deterministic polynomial-time reduction from 3SAT produces simple unweighted graphs that are three-colorable in the satisfiable case and have no independent set of size δ n otherwise, where n is the number of vertices.

papers.title: Hardness of finding large independent sets in three-colorable graphs

107.explainer: omega is the exponent in the cost n^omega of multiplying n x n matrices; every algebraic algorithm whose bottleneck is matrix multiplication (inverse, determinant, linear systems, many graph algorithms) inherits it. Since 1990 progress came from the laser method on Coppersmith-Winograd tensors and moved the bound only from 2.3755 to 2.3712. The 9/4 paper abandons that route: by Strassen's duality theorem omega is governed by 'tensor characters' (monotone ring homomorphisms on tensors), and the paper shows every character satisfies inequalities on the polynomial-multiplication tensors C(a,b) (concavity from a determinant filtration, a shifted tripling from a three-sector degeneration, each powered by a new Fourier-plus-quadratic-weights trick that separates blocks sharing one leg) which force a^{4/3} <= P(a,a) <= (2a-1)^{1/t}, hence t <= 3/4 and omega <= 9/4.
107.caveats: (a) Over C/char 0 only for 9/4; the every-field claim is only 2.371054886, an improvement of 0.000122 over Dupont et al.'s 2.371177. (b) The 9/4 proof is non-constructive (Strassen spectral duality + Schauder-Tychonoff-type fixed point): it yields no explicit algorithm or base size; arithmetic-model only, no bit complexity. (c) 'Outside finitely many positive characteristics' for 2.258: exceptional primes are not computed and that transfer is not in Lean. (d) The 2.258 paper's square proof rests on an 83-page argument with a C++/GMP certificate.
107.lean: main theorem formalized: ComparatorChallenges/MatrixMultiplication.lean pins omega(C) <= 9/4, alpha(C) > 93/200, rectangularOmega(C, 0.709) < 523/250 (solution OAI.LinearAlgebra.MatrixMultiplication.Main; the 9/4 proof is the ~10.9k-line AuxiliarySeparation subtree.
107.summary: Proves ω ≤ 9/4 over ℂ, giving O_ε(n^(9/4+ε)) arithmetic operations for square matrix multiplication. In characteristic zero, some inner dimension n^a with a > 0.465 permits n^(2+o(1)) rectangular multiplication. Further square bounds give ω < 2.258 outside finitely many positive characteristics and ω < 2.371054886006746 over every fixed field.

papers.title: An Upper Bound of 9/4 for the Matrix Multiplication Exponent
Complex Matrix Multiplication Below 2.258 and Rectangular Bounds
Staggered extraction for exact matrix multiplication over every field

108.explainer: The permanent looks like the determinant without signs, but is #P-hard; VP vs VNP (the algebraic P vs NP) asks whether it can be written as a polynomial-size determinant. For twenty years the best lower bound on that size was quadratic. The new idea is to extract from the permanent a degree-~k form in ~k^2 variables whose zero set is smooth, then use a polar-degree count showing any determinant (or limit of determinants) representing a smooth form of degree r in d variables needs size about (r-1)(d-1), which multiplies out to cubic.
108.caveats: Still polynomial; says nothing about VP vs VNP directly. The paper uses deep external algebraic geometry (Christ-He-Tyomkin arbitrary-characteristic Severi dimension theorem, Fantechi-Gottsche-van Straten), yet the Lean development (57 files, no 'Severi' identifier) claims the full statement with no extra axioms, so either it found another route or formalized these; I could not verify which. Constant 1/(5529600e) means the bound beats m^2/2 only for m in the millions. No public expert assessment of this specific result found as of 2026-10-07.
108.lean: main theorem formalized: PermanentCubic.lean (OAI.PermanentBorder.permanent_cubic_lower_bounds, both border and exact) proved in OAI/Algebra/Determinantal/Main.lean:384 (~21k lines), and SmoothInitialForm.lean for the general smooth-form bound; standard axioms. ABP consequences not formalized.
108.summary: Proves an Ω(n³) lower bound for the border determinantal complexity of the n× n permanent over ℂ. Even coefficientwise limits of determinants of affine-linear matrices require matrix size at least cn³, for an absolute c > 0 and all sufficiently large n; the same bound therefore holds for exact representations.

papers.title: A cubic lower bound for border determinantal complexity of the permanent

109.explainer: Harvey and van der Hoeven's 2019 O(n log n) algorithm was widely thought to be the end of the road. This claims you can shave a tiny power of log n by computing linear combinations of intermediate data (network-coding style) so that both the data shuffling on tapes and the FFT butterfly layers cost less than a full pass per level. Theoretically startling, practically irrelevant: GMP's crossover to Schonhage-Strassen is around tens of thousands of bits and this saving needs log n beyond any conceivable size.
109.caveats: kappa=2^{-182} makes the saving (lg n)^{2^{-182}} numerically indistinguishable from 1 for any physical n; the paper says constants and thresholds are 'extremely large'. Result is specific to the multitape TM bit model; it does not contradict the network-coding-conditional circuit lower bound because TM time T only gives circuits of size O(T log T). Uses XOR-coded data movement (address interchange in O(V u^tau)) which is itself a strong claim about TM transposition. Unformalized; the DFT family 130 reuses its phase network.
109.summary: Multiplies two n-bit integers exactly at every input length in deterministic worst-case time O(n(log n)^(1-κ)), with κ=2⁻¹⁸², on one fixed finite-alphabet Turing machine with finitely many one-dimensional tapes. This disproves the Schönhage–Strassen nlog n optimality conjecture in the ordinary multitape bit model.

papers.title: Integer multiplication below n log n

110.explainer: k-server is the abstract caching problem: k servers in a metric space, requests arrive online, minimize movement. After Bubeck-Coester-Rabani showed log^2 k is necessary in the worst case, the question was whether log^2 k suffices on every metric without dependence on the number of points; the claim says yes, by allocating fractional server mass on a hierarchy of partitions driven by the posterior of a hidden offline optimum.
110.caveats: Existence policy has no efficiency claim; the uniform version has polynomial per-request time only on finite rational metrics and an additive constant that 'may be enormous'. Matches the worst-case lower bound order, not the Omega(log k) universal lower bound on every metric. Builds on the withdrawn approach of Lee (heavy-ball protection), but claims to reprove what it needs. No public expert assessment of this specific result found as of 2026-10-07.
110.lean: main theorem formalized: KServer.lean and UniformKServer.lean, standard axioms
110.summary: Establishes a randomized competitive ratio O(log²(k+1)) for k-server on every metric space, matching the worst-case lower-bound order. One policy serves every finite oblivious request sequence, including on infinite unbounded metrics. On finite rational metrics, a uniform implementation has polynomial preprocessing and per-request bit cost in the input length and log (t+1) at request t, with a finite instance-dependent additive movement constant.

papers.title: Squared-logarithmic randomized k-server on arbitrary metrics
Uniform computation of the squared-logarithmic k-server bound

111.explainer: Prophet inequalities model posted-price mechanisms: accept or reject items online under a matroid constraint and compete with a prophet who knows everything. Knowing only one past sample per item is the realistic data regime; this shows a constant fraction is achievable even against the strongest adversary, though the constant is so small it is a qualitative statement.
111.caveats: Constant 2^{-310} is purely existential; no polynomial-time or oracle-efficient implementation is asserted.
111.lean: main theorem formalized: MatroidProphet.lean and MatroidSecretary.lean, standard axioms
111.summary: For every finite matroid known in advance, gives a distribution-independent online rule using one independent sample per element and earning a universal constant fraction of the expected offline optimum. Values are independent and nonnegative, with finite expected optimum. The guarantee holds even when the arrival-order adversary sees all samples, values, and the rule's entire random seed; no polynomial-time implementation is asserted.

papers.title: One Sample Suffices for Matroid Prophet Inequalities against an Almighty Adversary

112.explainer: Depth-3 circuit lower bounds are one of the few places where complexity theory proves explicit lower bounds, and beating 2^{c sqrt n} matters because 2^{omega(sqrt n)} lower bounds for depth-3 sit on known routes to bigger separations (Valiant's depth reduction). The trick is a restriction lemma that rewrites a restricted wide CNF as a signed sum of narrow CNFs with bounded total coefficient mass, independent of the number of clauses.
112.caveats: Superconstant improvement of the exponent's multiplier only (omega(sqrt n)), not n^{1/2+eps}; the hard function is a polynomial-evaluation language whose hard slices are found probabilistically and passed as input bits, which is standard but means the hardness lives in a sub-family. 20 pages and Lean-checked, so comparatively low risk.
112.lean: main theorem formalized: DepthThree.lean (exists_polynomial_time_language_depth_three_lower_bound), standard axioms
112.summary: Constructs a single language in deterministic polynomial time whose n-bit membership function requires 2^(ω(√n)) total gates in unbounded-fan-in OR–AND–OR circuits, at every sufficiently large input length. This crosses the square-root-exponent threshold for explicit depth-three Boolean circuit lower bounds.

papers.title: Beyond the Square-Root Exponent for Depth-Three Boolean Circuits

113.explainer: Counting perfect matchings exactly is #P-hard even for bipartite graphs, but JSV showed in 2001 that bipartite counts can be approximated by a Markov chain. General graphs (odd cycles, blossoms) defeated that approach for 35 years. If correct, approximate counting and near-uniform sampling of perfect matchings (dimer models, hafnians with 0/1 entries) become polynomial for every graph.
113.caveats: Polynomial bounds are not quantified as practical. The sampler uses a new state space (product of perfect-matching spaces on an enlarged colored graph) precisely to dodge the Stefankovic-Vigoda-Wilmes obstruction. Formal verification of a randomized polynomial-time machine with relative-error guarantees is unusual and strong evidence, if the statement is faithful. No public expert assessment of this specific result found as of 2026-10-07.
113.lean: main theorem formalized: MatchingFPRAS.lean (OAI.MatchingFPRAS.thm_main), MatchingEntropy.lean, MatchingEntropyBounds.lean, BinaryMatching.lean, SingletonLoopMatching.lean, TriangleFace.lean; standard axioms. The sharp global face-dimension bound is not part of the formalized statements.
113.summary: Gives a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme for counting perfect matchings in arbitrary finite simple graphs, with exact detection of zero counts. Also proves the perfect-matching entropy conjecture of Anari, Oveis Gharan, and Vinzant, bounding the maximum entropy of a matching law at every feasible edge-marginal vector in a loopless labelled multigraph, including boundary points.

papers.title: A Fully Polynomial Randomized Approximation Scheme for Perfect Matchings in General Graphs
Entropy and Face Dimension of the Perfect-Matching Polytope

114.explainer: Many combinatorial objects are 'common bases of two matroids' (bipartite perfect matchings, arborescences, colourful spanning trees). Approximately counting them in polynomial time unifies JSV and the log-concave-polynomial breakthrough for single matroids.
114.caveats: Oracle model; polynomial degrees unspecified. Builds on machinery shared with 113. No public expert assessment of this specific result found as of 2026-10-07; press coverage (officechai.com, startupfortune.com, 36kr) treats the release as unreviewed, and Altman described the headline claims as not yet confirmed by outside mathematicians. formalization.yaml lists review status 'unchecked'.
114.lean: partial formalization: CommonBasesFPRAS.lean covers the two-matroid result; the polymatroid paper is not formalized
114.summary: Gives a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme for counting common integer bases of two integral polymatroids of equal total rank, supplied by exact rank-value oracles. Capacities are binary-encoded, each integer vector counts once, and oracle calls and bit operations outside the oracles are polynomial on every execution. For matroids presented by independence oracles, the results also cover common independent sets of prescribed, unrestricted, or maximum cardinality, even when the ranks differ.

papers.title: An FPRAS for Common Integer Polymatroid Bases with Binary Capacities
Approximate counting of common bases of two matroids

115.explainer: Contingency tables with fixed margins are the null model behind Fisher's exact test and many network statistics. Statisticians sample them with MCMC heuristics of unknown mixing; a provably polynomial exact sampler is the theoretical guarantee those tools never had.
115.caveats: Exponents are 'deliberately large'; exact sampler polynomial only in expectation. No public expert assessment of this specific result found as of 2026-10-07; press coverage (officechai.com, startupfortune.com, 36kr) treats the release as unreviewed, and Altman described the headline claims as not yet confirmed by outside mathematicians. formalization.yaml lists review status 'unchecked'.
115.lean: main theorem formalized: ContingencyTables.lean covers both papers (exact/bounded-time sampling and cell-bounded FPRAS); standard axioms
115.summary: For nonnegative integer matrices with prescribed row and column sums, gives exact uniform sampling in expected polynomial bit time and almost-uniform sampling in worst-case polynomial bit time. The dimensions and binary-encoded margins are unrestricted. Also gives a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme for counting such tables with arbitrary individual cell bounds, including structural zeros, with polynomial cost on every execution.

papers.title: Exact Uniform Sampling of Contingency Tables with Arbitrary Margins
An FPRAS for Cell-Bounded Contingency Tables

116.explainer: Polynomial identity testing is the poster child of derandomization; in the noncommutative world you may plug in matrices. The claim is a single explicit set of matrices that certifies nonzeroness of every small formula without looking inside it.
116.caveats: The formalized one-point theorem omits the construction-time and dimension bounds. Matrix entries have bit length O(n s^2 log n), so a single test is polynomial but heavy.
116.lean: partial formalization: FormulaHitting.lean (universal hitting property only; bit-time and dimension bounds not asserted) and RationalHitting.lean; the positive-characteristic paper is not formalized
116.summary: For each characteristic, constructs in deterministic polynomial bit time a polynomial-dimensional matrix tuple detecting every nonzero division-free noncommutative formula of bounded size over any field of that characteristic. Rational formulas over ℚ also admit polynomial-size hitting lists whenever they have a defined rational-matrix evaluation.

papers.title: Uniform Matrix Hitting Points in Every Positive Characteristic
One Rational Matrix Hitting Point for Noncommutative Formulas
Polynomial Hitting Lists for Noncommutative Rational Formulas

117.explainer: Uniform sparsest cut is the graph-partitioning objective behind expansion, clustering and divide-and-conquer heuristics. Its best algorithm (ARV, sqrt(log n)) is famous; showing no constant factor is possible unless P=NP, and that the ARV SDP genuinely loses nearly sqrt(log n), would pin down the problem's approximability almost completely.
117.caveats: Hardness is ordinary NP-hardness for each fixed C, with polynomial degree depending on C. The headline NP-hardness (the larger claim) is the unformalized half. No public expert assessment of this specific result found as of 2026-10-07; press coverage (officechai.com, startupfortune.com, 36kr) treats the release as unreviewed, and Altman described the headline claims as not yet confirmed by outside mathematicians. formalization.yaml lists review status 'unchecked'.
117.lean: partial formalization: UniformSparsestCut.lean covers only the integrality-gap sequence; the NP-hardness paper is not formalized
117.summary: Proves that approximating Uniform Sparsest Cut within any fixed constant factor is NP-hard, even with nonnegative rational capacities and unit demands. The Goemans–Linial semidefinite relaxation also has integrality gaps of order at least √(log n)/(loglog n)³, approaching the square-root-logarithmic upper bound.

papers.title: Constant-factor hardness of uniform sparsest cut
Near-square-root logarithmic integrality gaps for uniform sparsest cut

118.explainer: Bin packing's configuration LP is the workhorse of cutting-stock software and was conjectured to be off by at most one bin. The claim is that the gap is unbounded and that no efficient algorithm can be within any fixed number of bins of optimal, which answers a textbook open problem.
118.caveats: Items have rational sizes with at most five per bin; instance sizes and encoding lengths grow with c. Combined with Hoberg-Rothvoss, the additive approximability of bin packing is now between omega(1) and O(log OPT). No public expert assessment of this specific result found as of 2026-10-07; press coverage (officechai.com, startupfortune.com, 36kr) treats the release as unreviewed, and Altman described the headline claims as not yet confirmed by outside mathematicians. formalization.yaml lists review status 'unchecked'.
118.lean: main theorem formalized: BinPackingGap.lean (OAI.BinPackingGap.main_results), ~159k lines, standard axioms
118.summary: Disproves the modified integer round-up conjecture of Scheithauer and Terno: the integral bin-packing optimum can exceed its configuration linear-programming value by an arbitrarily large additive constant. Approximating the optimum within any fixed additive constant is also NP-hard, even when every item exceeds 1/6 and each bin holds at most five items.

papers.title: Additive hardness and unbounded configuration gaps in bin packing

119.explainer: If you must compress n noisy-to-be bits into a single bit before they pass through a binary symmetric channel, which one-bit summary keeps the most information? The 'dictator' answer (just send one coordinate) was conjectured optimal in 2013 and resisted proof despite looking elementary. The claim proves it via a sharp contraction inequality along the noise semigroup, verified in Lean.
119.caveats: The Hellinger proof relies on 'finite exact arithmetic certificates' (computer-checked numerics) in the paper; Lean covers the main Courtade-Kumar result anyway. Information-theory community reaction not found. No public expert assessment of this specific result found as of 2026-10-07; press coverage (officechai.com, startupfortune.com, 36kr) treats the release as unreviewed, and Altman described the headline claims as not yet confirmed by outside mathematicians. formalization.yaml lists review status 'unchecked'.
119.lean: partial formalization: CourtadeKumar.lean and SoftChannel204.lean cover the sharp-contraction paper (Courtade-Kumar inequality with attainment, bias refinement, entropy production); the separate Hellinger paper is not formalized (the Courtade-Kumar bound itself is)
119.summary: Proves the Courtade–Kumar conjecture: among Boolean functions of independent uniform bits, a single coordinate retains the most mutual information after independent bit-flip noise. A stronger theorem treats randomized binary summaries at fixed initial information. The Hellinger conjecture is also proved for every Boolean output bias and noise correlation.

papers.title: Sharp binary-information contraction on the discrete cube
Hellinger contraction with arbitrary Boolean output bias

120.explainer: Bipartite matching joined max-flow in almost-linear time in 2022, but blossoms kept general matching at m sqrt(n) for 45 years. If correct, every graph's maximum matching can be found in near-linear time in theory; in practice Micali-Vazirani-style or push-relabel codes will remain faster for decades.
120.caveats: Monte Carlo (success 2/3, no certificate mentioned in the abstract); o(1) exponent loss unquantified and likely galactic, as for the almost-linear max-flow methods it presumably builds on. Unformalized. No public expert assessment of this specific result found as of 2026-10-07; press coverage (officechai.com, startupfortune.com, 36kr) treats the release as unreviewed, and Altman described the headline claims as not yet confirmed by outside mathematicians. formalization.yaml lists review status 'unchecked'.
120.summary: Gives a randomized algorithm finding an exact maximum-cardinality matching in any simple undirected graph in (n+m)^(1+o(1)) word time, with success probability at least 2/3. The time bound holds on every computation path. The same guarantees apply to finding a spanning subgraph with prescribed admissible vertex degrees, or deciding that none exists.

papers.title: Almost-Linear-Time Maximum-Cardinality Matching in General Graphs

121.explainer: Edit distance underlies diff tools, spell-checkers and DNA alignment. Exact computation is stuck at quadratic time under SETH; this says any fixed accuracy like 1.01x is achievable in almost-linear time. Bioinformatics aligners will not change, because the thresholds are huge and they already use banded or seeded heuristics, but it settles the theoretical question.
121.caveats: Asymptotic only: the algorithm runs exact DP below an accuracy-dependent length threshold the paper calls 'very large'; no polynomial dependence on 1/eps is claimed. Does not conflict with SETH since it is approximate.
121.lean: main theorem formalized: EditApproximation.lean, standard axioms
121.summary: For every fixed rational ε ∈ (0,1), gives a randomized (1+ε) approximation to unit-cost edit distance in worst-case expected time N^(1+o(1)), with success probability at least 2/3. The strings have total length N and polynomially bounded integer symbols. This is an asymptotic guarantee at fixed accuracy.

papers.title: An Almost-Linear Approximation Scheme for Edit Distance

122.explainer: Trace reconstruction asks how many randomly-deleted copies of a string you need to recover it, a toy model for DNA storage and sequencing. The claim brackets the answer between n^{log log n} and quasipolynomial, ending the hope for polynomial sample complexity in the worst case.
122.caveats: Lower and upper bounds are both new and both enormous jumps (from n^{1.5} to n^{log log n} below, and from exp(n^{1/5}) to quasipolynomial above); only the lower bound is machine-checked. The upper bounds therefore deserve more scrutiny. No public expert assessment of this specific result found as of 2026-10-07; press coverage (officechai.com, startupfortune.com, 36kr) treats the release as unreviewed, and Altman described the headline claims as not yet confirmed by outside mathematicians. formalization.yaml lists review status 'unchecked'.
122.lean: partial formalization: TraceReconstruction.lean covers the lower bounds only; both quasipolynomial upper-bound papers are unformalized
122.summary: At every fixed deletion probability in (0,1), reconstructing an arbitrary length-n binary string requires n^(Ω(loglog n)) independent traces, ruling out polynomial-sample reconstruction. A uniform decoder achieves quasipolynomial sample and running-time bounds for known fixed rational retention probabilities. When the deletion probability is at most n^(-ε) for fixed ε > 0, both bounds become polynomial in the input and parameter encoding.

papers.title: Uniform quasipolynomial-time trace reconstruction
A latest-anchor induction with spectrally compact masks for worst-case trace reconstruction
Quantitative lower bounds for trace reconstruction

124.explainer: Scheduling unit-length jobs with precedence constraints on 3 identical machines was one of the open problems at the back of Garey and Johnson's 1979 NP-completeness book. The claim decomposes optimal schedules into intervals whose job sets have bounded-size descriptions, so a dynamic program over polynomially many descriptions suffices. Real schedulers will not use an n^150020 algorithm; the news is that the problem is not NP-hard.
124.caveats: Exponent 150020 makes this purely a classification result. The paper says it resolves 'the polynomial-time side' of the question, i.e. it puts the problem in P; a 22-page paper plus Lean proof is a relatively checkable package. No public expert assessment of this specific result found as of 2026-10-07; press coverage (officechai.com, startupfortune.com, 36kr) treats the release as unreviewed, and Altman described the headline claims as not yet confirmed by outside mathematicians. formalization.yaml lists review status 'unchecked'.
124.lean: main theorem formalized: ThreeMachine.lean (OAI.ThreeMachine.main_theorem), solution OAI/Computability/Scheduling (53 files, ~18.6k lines), standard axioms; the Comparator challenge is not listed under status.main_results in formalization.yaml
124.summary: Resolves the three-processor unit-job scheduling problem of Garey and Johnson: a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm minimizes makespan for nonpreemptive unit-length jobs with arbitrary precedence constraints on three identical parallel machines. For an explicitly given precedence graph, it decides deadline feasibility exactly and constructs a feasible schedule.

papers.title: A Polynomial-Time Algorithm for Three-Machine Unit-Job Scheduling

125.explainer: k-median is the classic 'place k warehouses to minimize total distance' clustering objective. 1+2/e (about 1.736) is a known hardness floor; the claim is that a polynomial algorithm reaches it, which would close the problem's approximability completely.
125.caveats: Tightness is for the model with specified candidate facilities; the F=J (facilities at client locations) variant has a different lower-bound question. Polynomial depends on eps. No public expert assessment of this specific result found as of 2026-10-07; press coverage (officechai.com, startupfortune.com, 36kr) treats the release as unreviewed, and Altman described the headline claims as not yet confirmed by outside mathematicians. formalization.yaml lists review status 'unchecked'.
125.lean: main theorem formalized: MetricKMedian.lean, KMedianThreshold.lean, KMedianRecovery.lean, KMedianRefinedRecovery.lean; standard axioms
125.summary: Gives a deterministic polynomial-time (1+2/e+ε)-approximation for finite rational metric k-median with specified candidate facilities, for every fixed ε > 0. Assuming P ≠ NP, the optimal infimum approximation factor is 1+2/e.

papers.title: Single-exponential recovery and bounded-price strictness for metric k-median
The approximation threshold for metric k-median

126.explainer: Edmonds' matching polytope has exponentially many facets but matching is in P; Rothvoss showed no small LP describes it. This extends that to SDPs: no polynomial-size semidefinite program can express the matching polytope exactly, so 'just write an SDP' is not a shortcut around combinatorial matching algorithms.
126.caveats: The Lean-checked statement is weaker (superpolynomial) than the paper's exponential claim. The endpoint rho=1 has an O(n^2) factorization, so the shift is essential to the method.
126.lean: partial formalization: MatchingPSD.lean and MatchingAffineLift.lean state only superpolynomial lower bounds (> n^C for every C), not the exponential 2^{cn}
126.summary: Proves that every exact semidefinite lift of the perfect matching polytope has exponential size, answering Rothvoss's polynomial-size lift question negatively. The bound holds even for the positive semidefinite rank of its odd-cut slack matrix after any fixed shift 0 < ρ < 1, allowing arbitrary real positive semidefinite factors.

papers.title: Exponential PSD rank of positively shifted matching matrices

127.explainer: Total influence controls how learnable and how noise-stable a Boolean function is; O(d sqrt n) for degree-d threshold functions gives, e.g., agnostic learning of PTFs and noise-sensitivity bounds used in learning theory. The conjecture had resisted for 30 years despite its one-line statement.
127.caveats: Proves the asymptotic O(d sqrt n) form, not the exact extremizer statement (which is false). Short paper plus Lean proof makes it one of the more checkable entries.
127.lean: main theorem formalized: GotsmanLinial.lean, standard axioms
127.summary: Proves that a degree-at-most-d polynomial threshold function on the uniform n-dimensional Boolean cube has average sensitivity at most 8d√n, uniformly for 1 ≤ d ≤ n. Average sensitivity counts expected output changes under single-bit flips. This establishes the asymptotic Gotsman–Linial conjecture, allowing polynomial zeros with sign (0)=1.

papers.title: Average sensitivity of polynomial threshold functions

128.explainer: Shortest common superstring models genome assembly from reads and data compression. Factor 2 was the folklore target (what Greedy was conjectured to achieve); getting it with any polynomial algorithm closes a 35-year chase, even though production assemblers use de Bruijn/overlap graphs with very different objectives.
128.caveats: Does not resolve the Greedy conjecture; the paper itself cites a September 2026 preprint claiming Greedy is not a 2-approximation (unverified). Factor 2 is not known to be optimal.
128.lean: main theorem formalized: Superstring.lean (OAI.Superstring.main), standard axioms
128.summary: Gives a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm constructing a common superstring of length at most twice the optimum for every finite family of explicitly represented strings. The running time is polynomial in the full encoded input length, including symbol labels.

papers.title: A Polynomial-Time 2-Approximation for Shortest Common Superstring

129.explainer: Can a deterministic finite automaton that may move its head back and forth simulate a nondeterministic one with only polynomially more states? Sakoda and Sipser asked in 1978 and it became the flagship open problem of descriptional complexity. The claim answers 'no' using the Brauer diagram monoid: a 2DFA's repeated visits to a cell are captured by perfect matchings on ports, and matchings cannot faithfully encode products of arbitrary relations without exponentially many ports.
129.caveats: Alphabet size grows (exponentially) with the number of states, which is the standard Sakoda-Sipser setting, but the hard inputs are presumably long: since an exponential bound on polynomially long inputs would imply L/poly != NL (Kapoutsis), this cannot be such a bound, and no complexity-class consequence is claimed. Constants 1/127 and 1/31 in the exponent. 38 pages, Lean-checked. No public expert assessment of this specific result found as of 2026-10-07.
129.lean: main theorem formalized: TwoWayComplementation.lean, TwoWayDeterminization.lean, OneWayLiveness.lean; standard axioms
129.summary: Proves exponential lower bounds both for complementing two-way nondeterministic finite automata and for simulating one-way nondeterministic automata by two-way deterministic ones. The latter resolves the Sakoda–Sipser state-succinctness conjecture over growing finite alphabets; both results rule out polynomial state bounds independent of alphabet size.

papers.title: An exponential state lower bound for two-way nondeterministic complementation
An exponential two-way deterministic state lower bound for one-way liveness

130.explainer: The FFT's n log n operation count has never been proved optimal except in restricted models (bounded coefficients, unitary gates, well-conditioned steps). These papers show that with arbitrary exact complex constants it is not optimal: a fixed 2x2 unitary C = H diag(1,i) H has a tensor power C^(x)k computable in 2^k k^theta instead of k 2^k operations, via a finite network with a saving of Delta = 6.87e15 directional steps out of ~2.4e27 that is amplified by recursion. Good-Thomas reindexing turns F_L into a tensor product of small prime-length DFTs, each compiled (Newton/LDL^T + Toeplitz + dirty-workspace replay) into O(log^4 r) layers of monomials and copies of C on pairs; synchronized across axes, each layer becomes a direct sum of tensor powers of C, which is where the saving lands. Bluestein's chirp handles every n.
130.caveats: Model is the unrestricted (unbounded-coefficient, exact) linear/arithmetic model; consistent with Morgenstern and Ailon because it violates their hypotheses (coefficients, unitarity, conditioning). The family summary attaches '([Lean])' to the delta = 10^-13 all-n statement, but the Lean covers only the weaker subsequential nonuniform theorem (lean/docs/130.md says so plainly).
130.lean: partial formalization: the nonuniform subsequence theorem of paper 2 (Comparator challenge ComparatorChallenges/ExactFourier.lean, MainStatement; solution OAI.ExactFourier.main_theorem at OAI/Computability/FourierCircuit/Main.lean:277, 51 files / 19,103 lines, no sorry or axiom in the library by grep.
130.summary: Gives a deterministic length-n discrete Fourier transform algorithm using O(n(log n)^(1-δ)) operations for every n, with explicit δ=10⁻¹³. The model uses exact complex arithmetic, unrestricted coefficients and a supplied root of unity, and counts scalar preparation and logarithmic-word indexing.

papers.title: An explicit power saving for the exact discrete Fourier transform
Finite tensor savings and exact Fourier circuits

131.explainer: Network scientists generate random graphs with a given degree sequence (the configuration-model null) by repeatedly swapping edge endpoints. This proves that heuristic provably mixes in polynomial time for every degree sequence, which justifies a tool used in thousands of papers, though the n^8 bound is far too loose to set step counts.
131.caveats: n^8 is a worst-case bound; practical mixing is believed much faster. Simple undirected case only (directed/bipartite variants of KTV not claimed). No public expert assessment of this specific result found as of 2026-10-07; press coverage (officechai.com, startupfortune.com, 36kr) treats the release as unreviewed, and Altman described the headline claims as not yet confirmed by outside mathematicians. formalization.yaml lists review status 'unchecked'.
131.lean: main theorem formalized: SwitchChain.lean (mixing time, connectivity, spectral gap); the exact sampler is not formalized
131.summary: Resolves the simple-undirected Kannan–Tetali–Vempala conjecture: the lazy edge-switch chain mixes in O(n⁸) time for every graphical labeled degree sequence. The same degree-constrained graphs can also be sampled exactly uniformly by an almost-surely terminating algorithm with expected polynomial bit running time.

papers.title: Polynomial mixing of the switch chain for every graphical degree sequence

132.explainer: Sensitivity counts single-bit flips that change f; block sensitivity allows flipping disjoint groups. After Huang's 2019 proof that they are polynomially related, the natural guess was that the true relation is quadratic. The construction nests tournament-indexed predicates recursively so block sensitivity grows faster than sensitivity squared.
132.caveats: alpha is some fixed constant >2, not specified as large; gap between s^{2+} and Huang's s^4 remains. 11 pages and a small Lean development: among the easiest claims in the release to check.
132.lean: main theorem formalized: SensitivitySeparation.lean (OAI.Paper320.quantitative_separation), ~4.4k lines, standard axioms
132.summary: Constructs total Boolean functions with block sensitivity bs (f) ≥ s(f)^α for a fixed α > 2, disproving the quadratic strengthening of the Sensitivity Conjecture. Here s(f) counts influential individual-bit flips, while block sensitivity allows disjoint groups of bits to change together.

papers.title: A superquadratic separation between sensitivity and block sensitivity

133.explainer: k-dimensional WL is the canonical graph-isomorphism heuristic and the expressivity yardstick for graph neural networks (k-WL = k-GNN power). This says the n^k cost of higher-order WL is unavoidable, not an artifact of the refinement algorithm, so higher-order GNNs inherit the cost.
133.caveats: The unconditional lower bound is the time-hierarchy type (it follows from EXPTIME-hardness with k in the input plus padding), so it is real but of the 'diagonalization' flavor; it applies to deterministic sequential models only.
133.lean: main theorem formalized: ParityLifts.lean, WLIdentification.lean, WeisfeilerLeman.lean, VariableWL.lean (all four papers); standard axioms
133.summary: Proves unconditional n^(Ω(k)) deterministic time lower bounds for joint and separate k-dimensional Weisfeiler–Leman equivalence, for sufficiently large fixed k in the specified sequential adjacency-matrix models. With dimension as input, joint equivalence is EXPTIME-complete even on subcubic graphs; deciding whether refinement identifies a graph is also EXPTIME-complete.

papers.title: Parity lifts and bounded-treewidth witnesses for Weisfeiler–Leman equivalence
The complexity of identifying a graph by Weisfeiler–Leman refinement
Unconditional time lower bounds for Weisfeiler–Leman equivalence
Variable-dimension Weisfeiler–Leman equivalence on general and subcubic graphs

134.explainer: With complement allowed, regular expressions need surprisingly few nested stars: nobody had found a language needing two, and nobody could prove any fixed bound. Three nested stars always suffice, by encoding finite-monoid computations with affine updates and a prefix code of word pieces. For regex engine authors this is a curiosity: the expressions can be astronomically long.
134.caveats: Does not decide whether height 1 suffices (the headline generalized star-height problem); it proves a uniform bound of 3. Expression size unbounded.
134.lean: main theorem formalized: GeneralizedStarHeight.lean (OAI.GeneralizedStarHeight.main) for the bound 3, which subsumes the 13 and 4 papers; standard axioms
134.summary: Every regular language over a finite alphabet has a generalized regular expression with at most three nested Kleene stars, allowing union, concatenation and complement over the same alphabet. This establishes an absolute bound independent of automaton size, resolving the uniform-boundedness version of the generalized star-height problem.

papers.title: Finite Monoid Computations and a Uniform Generalized Star-Height Bound
Generalized Star Height at Most Four
Generalized Star Height at Most Three

135.explainer: Constant-depth arithmetic circuit lower bounds are the front line of algebraic complexity since LST 2021. Pinning homogeneous depth-5 complexity of iterated matrix multiplication at n^{Theta(sqrt n)} sharpens the picture, but stays far from general lower bounds.
135.caveats: Homogeneity is syntactic and essential; general (non-homogeneous) depth-5 is not covered. I could not confirm the exact prior state for depth 5 beyond the paper's own account.
135.lean: main theorem formalized: DepthFive.lean (lower and upper bounds), standard axioms
135.summary: Over every characteristic-zero field, the (1,1) entry of a product of n independent n× n variable matrices requires n^(Θ(√n)) gates in homogeneous depth-five sum–product circuits. This sharp bound allows shared gates and bottom linear forms involving all variables.

papers.title: Homogeneous depth-five lower bounds for iterated matrix multiplication

136.explainer: The PCP theorem made NP-hardness robust to a constant fraction of errors; this is the analogue for PPAD, the class of fixed-point problems like Nash equilibria. It means approximate equilibria that are allowed to be wrong in a constant fraction of places are still PPAD-hard with only polylogarithmic blow-up, tightening the case that equilibrium computation is genuinely hard.
136.caveats: Longest TCS manuscript in the release (147 pages), unformalized. Under ETH for PPAD it implies stronger lower bounds for approximate Nash, but those consequences stay conditional. No public expert assessment of this specific result found as of 2026-10-07; press coverage (officechai.com, startupfortune.com, 36kr) treats the release as unreviewed, and Altman described the headline claims as not yet confirmed by outside mathematicians. formalization.yaml lists review status 'unchecked'.
136.summary: Resolves the quasilinear PCP-for-PPAD conjecture. An End-of-Line instance of length N reduces to numerical circuit constraints of total length N(log N)^(O(1)) such that any polynomially encoded rational assignment satisfying all but a fixed fraction to fixed accuracy yields an endpoint solution. Such assignments always exist, giving robust local verification with only quasilinear size overhead.

papers.title: The PCP-for-PPAD conjecture: a quasilinear reduction

137.explainer: Ryan Williams' 2025 result that time t fits in sqrt(t) space was the year's big complexity surprise. For the restricted one-tape model the classic barrier was also sqrt(t); this claims t^{2/5}, suggesting the square root is not the natural limit.
137.caveats: Model-specific (one writable tape, supplied cap, accessor condition); answers Williams's question only for that model; unformalized.
137.summary: Determines the halting and finite-control outcome of a fixed deterministic one-writable-tape machine up to time T using O(T^(2/5)log^C(T+2)) space, improving the square-root exponent. Heads move at most one cell per step; finitely many read-only input heads are allowed. Initial contents are independent of T, and contents and input symbols have polylogarithmic-space access. Simulation time is unrestricted.

papers.title: Simulating One-Tape Time in Two-Fifths-Power Space

138.explainer: Subset Sum has been stuck at 2^{n/2} meet-in-the-middle since 1974 in the worst case, even though random instances fall to 2^{0.29n} with representation techniques. A worst-case 2^{0.49n} would break a 50-year barrier; cryptographic knapsacks are unaffected since they already rely on average-case lattice attacks.
138.caveats: Unformalized; word size 4(n+b+log n) bits is generous (Theta(n)-bit words) though standard for this problem; savings of 2^{0.01n} only. If correct it would also give (randomized) improvements for related problems (knapsack variants) reducing to worst-case Subset Sum. No public expert assessment of this specific result found as of 2026-10-07; press coverage (officechai.com, startupfortune.com, 36kr) treats the release as unreviewed, and Altman described the headline claims as not yet confirmed by outside mathematicians.
138.summary: Gives a uniform randomized classical algorithm for worst-case Subset Sum in ordinary O(2^(0.49n)) word-RAM time on polynomial-bit inputs, where n counts the integers. The time bound holds on every execution and success probability is at least 2/3 on every input. Inputs may repeat positive integers; words have O(n+b) bits for maximum input bit length b.

papers.title: Subset Sum in Time O(2^(0.49n))
A Low-Space Algorithm for Worst-Case Subset Sum

139.explainer: How many gradient evaluations does it take to sample from a nice log-concave distribution in d dimensions? Standard MCMC needs a power of d. The claim is that, information-theoretically, d^{eps} suffice for any eps, using recursively nested Gaussian-smoothed conditional means; practical samplers for Bayesian inference are not affected because the hidden computation is unbounded.
139.caveats: Query complexity only: computation between queries is unbounded and the construction uses approximation orders depending on eps, so C_eps is enormous and running time is not polynomial-bounded as claimed. Condition number fixed at 2.
139.lean: main theorem formalized: LogConcaveQuery.lean (upper C_eps d^eps and lower c log d), standard axioms
139.summary: For C² potentials with a supplied minimizer and I ⪯ ∇²V ⪯ 2I, proves that sampling within total variation 1/10 requires only C_ε d^ε exact value-and-gradient queries for every fixed ε > 0. The bound holds on every run, with unrestricted computation between queries. A logarithmic lower bound also holds, so the optimal power-law exponent in this oracle model is zero.

papers.title: Subpolynomial query complexity for well-conditioned log-concave sampling

140.explainer: With d^2 bits you can store the normal equations and solve regression from d samples; with less memory you must stream. This proves that below the d^2 threshold you pay an extra log(1/eps) factor in samples for exact Gaussian measurements, a clean memory-vs-data tradeoff relevant to streaming and on-device learning theory.
140.caveats: Six overlapping papers (301 pages) for one result; the summary's claim is narrow (noiseless, Gaussian design, uniform prior, finite-state learner). Matches the natural O(d log 1/eps)-sample low-memory upper bound, so the lower bound is tight in its regime.
140.lean: main theorem formalized: MemoryPrecision.lean, NoiselessRegression.lean, PosteriorReplicas.lean, GaussianFiniteEntropy.lean, GaussianInformation.lean, ProjectionMoments.lean, GaussianReplacement.lean, SubsphereCurrent.lean; standard axioms; some variant statements (3/5 success, dimension two) outside scope
140.summary: For fixed A > 0, a one-pass learner with Ad² persistent bits needs Ω_A(dlog (1/ϵ)) noiseless Gaussian samples to recover a unit vector to angular error 0 < ϵ ≤ 1/10 with probability 2/3, uniformly in accuracy for large d. Computation and randomized updates are unrestricted, but output uses only the terminal state, stopping index and fresh randomness.

papers.title: Memory and precision in noiseless Gaussian regression
Posterior replicas and conditional information in Gaussian regression
Localization costs and information growth for exact Gaussian observations
Projection moments, positive cap domination, and Riesz estimates on the sphere
Replacing Gaussian observations in memory-constrained inference
Subsphere methods for memory-sample lower bounds in noiseless Gaussian regression

141.explainer: Many geometric problems (graph drawing, Nash with 3 players, neural net training feasibility) are exists-R-complete, sitting somewhere between NP and PSPACE. Putting exists-R inside the counting hierarchy moves the upper bound well below PSPACE, using sign determination tricks in the spirit of PosSLP in CH.
141.caveats: Level 26 of the counting hierarchy is a structural result, not an algorithm; unformalized. No public expert assessment of this specific result found as of 2026-10-07; press coverage (officechai.com, startupfortune.com, 36kr) treats the release as unreviewed, and Altman described the headline claims as not yet confirmed by outside mathematicians. formalization.yaml lists review status 'unchecked'.
141.summary: Proves that the existential theory of the reals lies in the counting hierarchy. More generally, truth of existential–universal real sentences can be decided at one fixed level of that hierarchy, even when their integer polynomials are specified by arithmetic circuits.

papers.title: Existential–universal real sentences in the counting hierarchy

142.explainer: Randomized algorithms have factored polynomials over finite fields fast since 1970; the open question was whether randomness is needed. The claim says no: with auxiliary primes l where p is not a q-th power, the algebra can deterministically split factors, and analytic number theory (a uniform zero-free region for Hecke L-functions) guarantees such primes are small. Crypto and coding libraries keep using Cantor-Zassenhaus.
142.caveats: Correctness rests on an unformalized analytic number theory theorem in another family (029), which itself claims the infinitude part of Artin's primitive root conjecture for all admissible bases, a landmark claim in its own right; I classify the kind as 'conditional' on that companion. Exponent 10^12 makes it purely theoretical. As a special case it would give a deterministic polynomial-time way to find quadratic nonresidues mod p, long open without GRH. No public expert assessment of this specific result found as of 2026-10-07.
142.lean: none (and the companion family 029, an Artin-primitive-root infinitude result, has no lean/docs page either)
142.summary: Gives a uniform deterministic algorithm that completely factors every nonzero dense degree-n polynomial over a prime field 𝔽ₚ, including multiplicities, in bit complexity polynomial in (n+1)log p. The prime is supplied in binary. No randomness, integer-factorization or primitive-root oracle, or GRH assumption is required.

papers.title: Deterministic Polynomial Factorization over Prime Fields

143.explainer: A limit cycle is an isolated closed orbit of a planar polynomial ODE; Hilbert asked how many a degree-d system can have. The proof follows the return map around each cycle, writes it as a chain of local 'passages' near singular points whose asymptotic expansions can degenerate at different rates as coefficients vary, and shows that the auxiliary equations have only finitely many isolated solutions even when every variable, including the coefficients, is free; compactness of the coefficient space then yields one bound per degree. The quintic Liénard result is a separate, much more concrete count that is fully machine-checked.
143.caveats: The landmark half (uniform bound, 160 pp.) is NOT formalized; lean/docs/143.md and the comparator challenge QuinticLienard (OAI.QuinticLienard.main, in formalization.yaml main_results, standard axioms only) cover only the quintic Liénard bound of 2. The uniform bound is purely existential, gives no estimate of B(d) even for d=2, and rests on a new 'absolute isolated-zero finiteness' criterion for asymptotic expansions on nested complex domains — exactly the kind of degenerate-asymptotics argument where Dulac's 1923 proof failed.
143.summary: Resolves the uniform boundedness assertion in Hilbert's sixteenth problem: the number of isolated periodic orbits of a real planar polynomial vector field is bounded by a finite constant depending only on its degree. For classical quintic Liénard systems, the exact maximum is two limit cycles.

papers.title: Uniform bounds for planar polynomial limit cycles
Two limit cycles for quintic Liénard systems

144.explainer: Spectral theory of a measure-preserving map asks what unitary operator f↦f∘T looks like; 'simple Lebesgue' means it is exactly the bilateral shift on one copy of L^2 of the circle — the same spectrum as an i.i.d. coin-flip system but with multiplicity one instead of infinity. The construction builds the map as a limit of smooth conjugated twists whose Fourier signals are transported so that one observable's orbit becomes orthonormal and complete.
144.caveats: The paper itself says the historical real-line question recorded by Ulam differs from the probability-space form solved here. Lean challenge ThreeTorus.lean exists with docs/144.md (standard axioms), but it is not listed in formalization.yaml status.main_results. Only 30 pages for a problem open since the 1930s–60s; construction uses explicit volume-preserving passages between integrable twists (Anosov–Katok-style). No public expert reaction found.
144.summary: Resolves the probability-preserving form of Banach's simple Lebesgue-spectrum problem within smooth dynamics. A smooth volume-preserving diffeomorphism of the standard-volume three-torus has simple Lebesgue spectrum on its entire complex mean-zero L² space: the bilateral iterates of one real observable form an orthonormal basis of that space.

papers.title: A smooth three-torus diffeomorphism with simple Lebesgue spectrum

145.explainer: Mixing says two events become independent when far apart in time; Rokhlin asked whether three or more events then automatically become jointly independent. The proof assumes a least failing order k, reduces (via a Pinsker/Thouvenot-type reduction) to a zero-entropy finite-alphabet process with a non-product limit joining whose proper marginals are independent, then iterates limits into an ordered family of 'array laws' and shows by operator and cancellation estimates that such a joining must be product — contradiction.
145.caveats: Lean challenge Rokhlin.lean (OAI.Rokhlin.mixing_all_finite_orders) matches the statement faithfully and uses only propext/Quot.sound/Classical.choice, but is not in formalization.yaml main_results; I could not build it. Only 40 pages for one of ergodic theory's most famous problems. Used as an input by family 154 and the 144 paper. No public expert reaction found.
145.summary: Proves that every invertible mixing probability-preserving transformation is mixing of all finite orders, resolving Rokhlin's multiple-mixing problem for a single transformation. Correlations among any finite collection of measurable sets converge to the product of their measures whenever all pairwise time separations diverge.

papers.title: Rokhlin's multiple-mixing problem for one transformation

146.explainer: The standard map is the textbook model of Hamiltonian chaos; numerics have always shown a chaotic sea but no one could prove it has positive area because elliptic islands keep appearing. By Pesin's formula, entropy for area equals the integral of the positive Lyapunov exponent, so the paper needs derivative growth on a positive-area set at every large k, controlling the recurrent loss of expansion near the critical lines where cos 2πx vanishes.
146.caveats: Claims a full parameter tail [k0,∞), stronger than the conjecture, but k0 is not explicit; no claim of ergodicity or a.e. positive exponents. Lean challenges StandardMapEntropy/Lyapunov/Components exist (docs/146.md), not in yaml main_results. 45 pages is short given decades of failed attempts on the elliptic-island problem. No public expert reaction found.
146.summary: Proves that the standard sine map on the two-dimensional torus has positive metric entropy with respect to area for every sufficiently large positive parameter. This establishes Sinai's positive-parameter-measure conjecture for the original family, with the stronger conclusion of a full parameter tail.

papers.title: Positive Metric Entropy for the Standard Map at Large Parameters

147.explainer: In a billiard, a caustic is a curve that trajectories stay tangent to; ellipses have a whole family (confocal ellipses). The theorem shows that having such caustics fill a neighborhood of the boundary continuously already forces analyticity and then the elliptic shape, a 'local integrability ⇒ ellipse' rigidity result.
147.caveats: Not the full Birkhoff conjecture: needs a full continuous collar of caustics/invariant curves near the boundary (a Cantor family, which is what KAM gives generically, does not count). No Lean. 146-page main paper plus 27-page bridge. No public expert reaction found.
147.summary: Resolves the near-boundary Birkhoff conjecture for smooth strictly convex planar billiards of positive curvature. Such a billiard is an ellipse whenever a full grazing annulus is continuously foliated by individually invariant essential curves. A continuous physical collar of smooth closed convex caustics also suffices.

papers.title: Continuous Phase Foliations Create Analytic Caustic Collars
Rigidity of Smooth Billiards with a Continuous Caustic Collar

148.explainer: A self-similar measure is the law of a random composition of contractions; if different words give the same map you lose entropy, and the conjecture says that is the only way dimension can drop. In particular it implies the exact-overlaps conjecture on the line: with no exact coincidences, dimension is the naive entropy/Lyapunov ratio. The proof compares a finite law's exact entropy with its entropy at a grid scale, shows hidden information must be witnessed by fair two-point laws at finer scales (an estimate independent of the smallest gap), and conditions on block symbol counts so each block's contraction is fixed and translations identify the composed map.
148.caveats: Main theorem is in formalization.yaml main_results (SelfSimilar.json, OAI.EntropyRateDimension.entropy_rate_dimension, standard axioms) — among the strongest verification signals in the group. Dimension only; absolute continuity not addressed. 22 pages. No public expert reaction found.
148.summary: For every self-similar measure on the line generated by finitely many contracting similarities, proves dim_Hμ=min{1,h_(RW)/χ}, where h_(RW) is the entropy rate of random composed maps and χ the average logarithmic contraction. This resolves the entropy-rate dimension conjecture without a separation assumption, allowing exact overlaps and unequal contraction ratios.

papers.title: The entropy-rate dimension formula for self-similar measures on the line

149.explainer: Chemical reaction networks with mass-action kinetics are polynomial ODEs; weak reversibility (every reaction can be undone by a chain of reactions) was conjectured to keep every species from dying out or blowing up. The result builds a compact convex absorbing region in each conservation class, giving uniform lower and upper concentration bounds after a transient.
149.caveats: Lean (MassAction challenge, docs/149.md) covers the boundedness/persistence statement with initial-state-dependent bounds, not the classwise uniform permanence of the 13-page main paper. Fixed rate constants only (not the time-dependent-rate version sometimes stated). Very short papers for conjectures that resisted CRN theory for decades. No public expert reaction found.
149.summary: Proves the permanence conjecture for every finite weakly reversible mass-action system with fixed positive rate constants. Every positive stoichiometric compatibility class, even an unbounded one, has a common compact convex forward-invariant absorbing set. All positive trajectories in that class therefore eventually share positive lower and finite upper concentration bounds.

papers.title: Uniform Permanence in Weakly Reversible Mass-Action Systems
Boundedness and persistence of weakly reversible mass-action systems

150.explainer: A billiard in a triangle is the simplest system with no curvature to create chaos; with rational angles the motion splits into invariant surfaces, but with an irrational angle it was expected (and numerically debated) to be ergodic. Unfolding reflections turns trajectories into straight lines on a flat surface with cone points; the paper's main issue is the low regularity there.
150.caveats: Ergodicity is formalized (IrrationalTriangleBilliard challenge, docs/150.md, standard axioms; not in yaml main_results); weak mixing is not. Two papers of 12 and 13 pages for a problem considered very hard — length is a red flag that warrants scrutiny of the low-regularity analysis (the paper leans on Forni–Moll analytic framework for flat surfaces with cone points). Claims quantum-ergodicity corollaries. No public expert reaction found.
150.summary: Proves that the billiard flow in every nondegenerate Euclidean triangle with at least one angle irrational relative to π is weakly mixing for normalized area times uniform direction. This strengthens ergodicity on the entire irrational-angle class, with no genericity or Diophantine restrictions.

papers.title: Weak mixing of triangular billiards with an irrational angle
Ergodicity of triangular billiards with an irrational angle

151.explainer: Entropy measures how fast orbits separate; homology growth was conjectured to force entropy, as Yomdin proved for C^∞ maps. Here one sphere coordinate usually squares (z↦z^2, giving the factor 2 on H_2), a circle 'clock' slows down near one reading, and auxiliary sphere 'registers' store small signals that cancel the high winding; C^1 is just enough regularity to hide the growth from orbit counting.
151.caveats: Noninvertible map; the C^1 diffeomorphism case (the version many authors mean) remains open. Lean challenge C1EntropyCounterexample (Problem340) formalizes the existence statement with the manifold concretely S^1×(S^2)^{q+1} embedded in Euclidean space and C^1 via local extensions — a faithful encoding; not in yaml main_results. No public expert reaction found.
151.summary: Constructs a noninvertible C¹ self-map of a compact smooth manifold with zero topological entropy but eigenvalue 2 on second homology. This disproves the homological entropy lower bound for general C¹ self-maps: homological growth need not force positive orbit complexity.

papers.title: A C^1 Counterexample to the Entropy Conjecture

152.explainer: Any abstract measure-preserving system can be asked: is it secretly a smooth volume-preserving map on a manifold? Entropy was the only known obstruction; this gives an example with zero entropy and still no smooth model, so the realization problem has a new, non-entropy obstruction.
152.caveats: Lean (SmoothObstruction, docs/152.md) only proves the finite-entropy version; the zero-entropy conclusion, which is the actual point, is outside the formalized statement. Smooth model here means positive smooth volume; does not exclude models preserving other measures. No public expert reaction found.
152.summary: Constructs a zero-entropy ergodic invertible transformation of a standard nonatomic probability space that is not measurably conjugate to any C^∞ diffeomorphism preserving a strictly positive smooth probability density on a compact finite-dimensional manifold. One example rules out every finite dimension.

papers.title: A zero-entropy system without a smooth positive-volume model

153.explainer: A Bernoulli convolution is the law of Σ±λ^n; for λ>1/2 it is usually smooth, and only Pisot reciprocals were known to give a singular (fractal-like) law. The paper links singularity to how well λ is approximated by special algebraic units and verifies the approximation for quartic Salem numbers, whose conjugates on the unit circle defeat the classical Fourier argument.
153.caveats: The 'classification' is equivalent-but-ineffective (an infinite approximation condition), so the summary's 'classifies' is weaker than it sounds; the concrete new content is singularity at quartic Salem reciprocals. Unformalized; no family Lean docs. A first non-Pisot singular Bernoulli convolution would be a major event; scrutinize. No public expert reaction found.
153.summary: Classifies singular and absolutely continuous unbiased Bernoulli convolutions for every λ ∈ (0,1) by an infinite, one-sided approximation condition using explicit finite sets of algebraic units. It also proves singularity at reciprocals of every quartic Salem number in (1,2), giving examples beyond reciprocal Pisot parameters.

papers.title: Arithmetic classification and non-Pisot singularity for Bernoulli convolutions

154.explainer: Multiple ergodic averages are the dynamical engine behind Szemerédi's theorem; convergence in L^2 is known, but almost-everywhere convergence beyond two functions is a long-standing problem. Mixing alone identifies the limit (via Rokhlin multiple mixing); convergence comes from a harmonic-analysis oscillation estimate for the trilinear Hilbert transform transferred to the dynamical system.
154.caveats: Depends on two companion results: Rokhlin multiple mixing (family 145) and an L^3 bound for the trilinear Hilbert transform from a different family in the release (outside this group) — itself a famous open problem; the triple-slopes paper is 'a proof by reference' to those manuscripts. The main arbitrary-length paper says triple convergence at distinct slopes follows 'without a mixing assumption' from the companion oscillation estimate — that would be a much bigger claim (Furstenberg's triple problem for all systems) buried in a citation. Unformalized.
154.summary: Proves almost-everywhere convergence of consecutive multiple ergodic averages of every finite length for invertible mixing probability-preserving transformations. For each fixed tuple of bounded functions, the limit is the product of their integrals, along all positive averaging lengths. No mixing rate or standardness assumption on the probability space is required.

papers.title: Pointwise Multiple Ergodic Averages for Mixing Transformations
Pointwise convergence of fourfold ergodic averages for mixing transformations
Triple ergodic averages with distinct integer slopes
Pointwise convergence of triple ergodic averages for mixing transformations

155.explainer: The periodic tiling conjecture said any shape that can tile space by translations can also do so periodically; Greenfeld and Tao killed it in some huge dimension in 2022, leaving open how low the failure goes. This paper shows it fails already in Z^3 and R^3, which is optimal since Z and Z^2 are known to always admit periodic tilings. The trick is to encode a 'p-adic Sudoku' whose solutions exist but can never be vertically periodic into a system of tiling equations over Z^2 × (a cyclic group), merge them into one tile, and then 'unfold' the cyclic factor into the third integer coordinate; a marked-cube rigidity argument carries it to real translations.
155.caveats: Strong plausibility signals: short (26 pp), follows the published Greenfeld–Tao Sudoku/tiling-equation strategy closely, and the formal statement is stronger than the paper's theorem (includes minimality). Novel parts are making the finite factor cyclic (pairwise coprime orders) and a rigidification Z^2 × Z/QZ → Z^3 → R^3. The tile is presumably astronomically large (p > 200, N = p^2, extra primes) — no explicit size given. Lean definitions of 'tiles' (bijection T × A → G) and 'fully periodic' look faithful.
155.lean: main theorem formalized — OAI.PeriodicTilingThree.periodic_tiling_counterexample_and_minimality, statement at lean/ComparatorChallenges/PeriodicTilingThree.lean line 52 (solution OAI/Geometry/PeriodicTiling/Counterexample.lean); covers both the Z^3 and the R^3 (a.e.
155.summary: Constructs a finite translational tile in ℤ³ that tiles space but admits no fully periodic tiling, disproving the periodic tiling conjecture in the smallest possible lattice dimension. Its unit-cube thickening gives the same counterexample in ℝ³, even with arbitrary real translation vectors.

papers.title: A translational tile with no fully periodic tiling in dimension three

156.explainer: Borsuk asked whether any bounded set in d-space can be chopped into d+1 pieces each of strictly smaller diameter; it is false in high dimension, and the record lowest dimension was 63 just months earlier. Here the set is all lines through the origin in R^4, represented as projector matrices: two projectors are at maximal distance exactly when the lines are orthogonal.
