A cover by 10 smaller pieces would give a partition of unity on RP^3 where orthogonal lines never share a support label; a mod-2 degree argument forces the label-support complex to be a tetrahedral cycle with rigid local structure, and a finite (Lean-checked) combinatorial case analysis shows no such 10-label structure exists.
156.caveats: Jump from 63 to 9 is enormous and the witness is a classical object (the projector/Veronese embedding of RP^3 used by Kahn–Kalai expositions) — surprising that nobody checked it, but the obstruction is topological (mod-2 degree, odd map on symmetric matrices, Walkup-type triangulation constraints) rather than Frankl–Wilson counting, which is a genuinely different route. Proof is short (18 pp) and fully formalized, including the finite case analysis; this is the most credible of the batch.
156.lean: main theorem formalized — OAI.BorsukNine.main_theorem, statement at lean/ComparatorChallenges/BorsukNine.lean line 25 (solution OAI/Geometry/Borsuk/Counterexample.lean): IsCompact X ∧ X ⊆ trace-one symmetric ∧ diam X = √2 ∧ ¬(∃ ten subsets of X covering X each of diam < √2).
156.summary: Constructs a compact subset of ℝ⁹ that cannot be covered by ten sets of strictly smaller diameter, disproving Borsuk's covering assertion already in dimension nine. The example consists of rank-one orthogonal projectors onto lines in ℝ⁴, with the Frobenius metric.

papers.title: A nine-dimensional counterexample to Borsuk's covering assertion

157.explainer: Hadwiger's conjecture (1943) says a graph needing t colours must contain a K_t minor; it generalizes the Four Colour Theorem and is perhaps the central open problem of graph minor theory. The claimed counterexamples have no three pairwise non-adjacent vertices, so they need at least n/2 colours, yet the construction (random sampling of algebraically defined 'holes' whose triangle-freeness comes from a parity identity) ensures there are no large 'connected matchings', which caps the clique-minor size at about 0.35n. Separately, and Lean-verified, the family proves the linear relaxation: χ_list(G) ≤ C·h(G) for an absolute C, via stable-set sampling into colour bins plus a recursive connectivity/routing argument.
157.caveats: The headline claims (Hadwiger and Colin de Verdière counterexamples) are the least verified: 104 + 131 pages of heavy, novel probabilistic/algebraic machinery (tensor-certified 'holes', Boolean moment matrices, container/entropy supersaturation, weak regularity) with no formalization and no public expert check found. A counterexample here would also settle in the negative the long-studied α ≤ 2 case and FGS connected-matching conjecture — extraordinary; treat as unverified.
157.lean: partial formalization — only paper 3 (linear list bound) is formalized: OAI.LinearListHadwiger.main_theorem, statement at lean/ComparatorChallenges/ListHadwiger.lean line 30 (∃ C ≥ 1, ∀ finite nonempty G, χ_list(G) ≤ C·h(G)).
157.summary: Disproves Hadwiger's conjecture even for fractional coloring: arbitrarily large finite simple graphs with independence number at most two satisfy χ_f(G) > h(G), where h(G) is the largest clique-minor order. Also disproves the fractional Colin de Verdière chromatic bound χ_f(G) ≤ μ(G)+1. In the positive direction, every finite nonempty graph satisfies χ_(list)(G) ≤ C h(G) for a universal constant C.

papers.title: A counterexample to Hadwiger's conjecture
A counterexample to the Colin de Verdière chromatic conjecture
A linear list-coloring bound in terms of the Hadwiger number

158.explainer: The Hadwiger–Nelson problem asks how many colours are needed so no two points exactly 1 apart share a colour; since 2018 the answer was known to be 5, 6 or 7. This proves 5 is impossible without exhibiting a finite graph: first it shows any proper colouring can be converted, by averaging over algebraic rotations and translations and a rigidity theorem about invariant measures on characters, into a measurable colouring that is proper almost everywhere. Then, for measurable colourings, it shows locally at most two colours meet along 'interfaces', builds a cycle of colours around a point by planar topology, and rules out cycles of length 3, 4 and 5, the last case by fitting a Moser spindle into a region that uses only three colours.
158.caveats: Very clean formal statement — if the Comparator check is sound, this is decisive. Surprising features: it avoids any explicit finite graph (searches by SAT have struggled even to shrink 5-chromatic graphs), uses ergodic-theoretic rigidity to pass from arbitrary to measurable colourings (a direction long considered hard; Falconer's measurable ≥5 did not transfer), so expert scrutiny of Thm 1.3 is the key. Formal proof size (~15k lines) seems modest for the Furstenberg–Zimmer/spectral machinery claimed, worth checking how much Mathlib covers.
158.lean: main theorem formalized — OAI.EuclideanFiveColor.no_proper_five_coloring, statement at lean/ComparatorChallenges/EuclideanFiveColor.lean line 10 (¬∃ c : ℂ → Fin 5 with c x ≠ c y whenever ‖x − y‖ = 1; arbitrary functions, no measurability); solution OAI/Geometry/PlaneColoring/Five.lean line 124.
158.summary: Proves that every five-coloring of the Euclidean plane has a monochromatic pair at distance one, with no restriction on the color classes. This advances the Hadwiger–Nelson problem: together with the classical seven-coloring, only six and seven remain possible chromatic numbers of the plane.

papers.title: The Euclidean plane is not five-colorable

159.explainer: Szemerédi's theorem says dense sets contain long arithmetic progressions; Erdős's $5000 question is whether sets as sparse as 'reciprocal sum diverges' (e.g. the primes) must too, which needs a density bound decaying faster than 1/(log N)^{1+eps}. Before this, only 3-term progressions were that strong (Kelley–Meka); for k>=5 the best bound saved only a power of log log N. The paper runs a density-increment iteration on 'triangular polynomial cells' and shows the precision lost at each weight depends only on higher-weight data, so O(log 1/alpha) increments cost only polynomially in log(1/alpha), giving exp(-c(log N)^eps). Dyadic summation then gives the Erdős statement.
159.caveats: 198-page single manuscript built on the Leng–Sah–Sawhney quasipolynomial inverse theorem and Schoen–Sisask almost-periodicity as black boxes, plus many new appendices (shift comparison, constrained sampling, cube comparison, relative lifting). The headline Erdős statement is (per the release) machine-checked in Lean without extra axioms, which is the strongest evidence here, but the formal statement only certifies the qualitative corollary via a weaker (log log N)^{1+eta} density bound — the paper's quantitative Theorem 1.1 (exp(-c(log N)^eps) for all…
159.lean: partial formalization — The Erdős corollary is formalized: OAI.Erdos3.manuscriptReciprocalProgressionTheorem in ComparatorChallenges/ErdosReciprocal.lean line 31 (∀ A : Set ℕ, ¬Summable(1/n on A) → ∀ k, HasAP A k with d>0).
159.summary: Proves Erdős's conjecture that every set of positive integers with divergent reciprocal sum contains arithmetic progressions of every finite length. Quantitatively, for each fixed k ≥ 3, every subset of {1,…,N} with no nonconstant k-term progression has size at most CₖNexp[-cₖ(log N)^(εₖ)], with positive constants depending only on k.

papers.title: Quasipolynomial Bounds for Arithmetic Progressions

160.explainer: Van der Waerden numbers measure how long an interval you can colour without a monochromatic k-term progression; for two colours the best constructions gave only about k·2^k, and Erdős asked whether growth is genuinely faster than any exponential c^k. The construction maps a cyclic group into high-dimensional tori (D ~ k^{1/10} coordinates), colours by coarse cells so that every progression is either colour-balanced or nearly affine, then randomly flips colours by squared-norm bands (Behrend-style) so affine progressions also break; counting the few possible patterns lets a union/local-lemma bound kill all progressions, giving k^{ck} for two colours and a digit-product boost for more colours.
160.caveats: Short (25 pp), elementary-probabilistic construction (Behrend-type squared-norm geometry on Z/q^D Z with LCM dilation, Bernoulli flips, local lemma) and its exact headline statement is formalized and listed among the release's main formal results — this is among the best-supported claims in the batch. The W definition in Lean uses sInf, so a lower bound on W also implicitly needs finiteness; docs say finiteness is proved. Constant c = 1e-5 is tiny and the threshold K_0 ineffective/unspecified.
160.lean: main theorem formalized — OAI.QuantitativeVanDerWaerden.uniform_lower_bound in ComparatorChallenges/QuantitativeVanDerWaerden.lean line 26: ∃ K, ∀ k ≥ K, ∀ r ≥ 2, k^{(1/100000)·k·Nat.log 2 r} < W r k, with W defined as sInf of Ramsey interval lengths.
160.summary: Resolves Erdős's superexponential-growth question for van der Waerden numbers. If W_r(k) is the least interval length forcing a monochromatic k-term progression in every r-coloring, then W_r(k) > k^(ck⌊log₂ r⌋) for an absolute c > 0, all r ≥ 2 and sufficiently large k, uniformly in r. In particular, W_r(k)^(1/k) → ∞ for each fixed r.

papers.title: Quantitative Superexponential Bounds for van der Waerden Numbers

161.explainer: Sidorenko's conjecture says a random graph minimizes the count of any bipartite pattern among graphs of a given edge density; it underpins supersaturation and quasirandomness theory and had been verified for many structured families. The paper picks a 35-vertex incidence graph of a triple system in which each point pair lies in exactly two triples, so a sign model on pairs produces a four-incidence parity correlation. Using kernels built from half-rank symmetric-matrix differences over a large finite field, it makes that correlation contribute a negative correction to the pattern density, then dilutes, symmetrizes and samples a finite host graph that inherits the strict deficit.
161.caveats: The host graph is purely existential (q -> infinity limit with a fixed large dimension D), not a computer certificate, and no numerical size of G is given; one cannot check the counterexample by direct computation. Proof is 51 pages of finite-field/Lagrangian counting estimates (singular-configuration bound in Sections 5-7 is the delicate part). The forcing-conjecture disproof is not Lean-checked. If the Lean build is sound, the Sidorenko disproof itself is machine-verified, which makes this far more credible than an unformalized claim.
161.lean: main theorem formalized — OAI.SidorenkoCounterexample.main in lean/ComparatorChallenges/SidorenkoCounterexample.lean (statement at line 41; H hard-coded from the 22 faces; homDensity counts all maps; strict inequality vs edgeDensity^66); solution module OAI.Combinatorics.Sidorenko.RandomHost (35 files, ~23.8k lines).
161.summary: Disproves Sidorenko's conjecture with a connected bipartite pattern on 35 vertices and 66 edges that occurs less frequently than in a random graph of the same edge density. The same pattern disproves the forcing conjecture of Skokan and Thoma: matching its density and the edge density of a constant graphon need not force quasirandomness.

papers.title: A counterexample to Sidorenko's conjecture

162.explainer: Ryser's conjecture generalizes König's theorem: an r-partite hypergraph should be coverable by (r-1) times its maximum matching size; for intersecting hypergraphs that means r-1 vertices suffice, which truncated projective planes show is tight. The paper starts from the affine plane over F_q with one part per direction (covering number q) and randomly splits and merges a few lines so that every pair of point-edges still meets, while a stability theorem for near-covers of prime planes plus incidence counting rule out any cover of size q; the covering number becomes q+1 = r, the maximum possible.
162.caveats: Asymptotic: no explicit rank or hypergraph is given, the prime thresholds q0, s0, n0(s) are existential, so the smallest counterexample rank is unknown (could be astronomically large). Relies on the Szőnyi–Weiner stability theorem for prime planes and on probabilistic constructions; paper 2 imports elementary estimates from paper 1. Small ranks (r<=5, and linear intersecting r<=9) remain consistent with the conjecture. Lean formalization of both main theorems is the strongest credibility signal. No public expert reaction found.
162.lean: main theorem formalized — BalancedRyser.lean (OAI.Balanced.main_result, line 39; MainResult def line 36) matches paper 1 incl. balanced parts and non-isolation; RyserOddExtensions.lean (OAI.RyserOdd.eventualOddFailures_and_infinite, line 61) matches paper 2's theorem.
162.summary: Disproves Ryser's covering conjecture by constructing intersecting (q+1)-partite, (q+1)-uniform hypergraphs with covering number q+1, rather than the predicted bound q, for every sufficiently large prime q. A separate construction over extension fields also disproves Gyárfás's monochromatic tree-cover conjecture.

papers.title: Balanced counterexamples to Ryser's conjecture at prime orders
A counterexample to Ryser's covering conjecture

164.explainer: Colour the integers with finitely many colours: Hindman showed you always find a set whose subset sums are one colour, and multiplicative versions follow by exponentiating, but asking for sums and products together in the same colour was open even for {x, y, x+y, xy}. The proof chooses products of widely separated blocks so products are already monochromatic (Ramsey plus finite sums), then must force the sums into the same colour: it models each colour class by piecewise nilsequences ('Prediction'), and picks rational scale adjustments from a fixed finite list so predicted colour stays positive after all needed additive shifts ('Alignment'), with success probability independent of model complexity.
164.caveats: Unformalized 70-page qualitative argument with heavy higher-order Fourier machinery: Green–Tao–Ziegler inverse theorem (citing a 2024 erratum and a 2026 revision), Tao–Ziegler concatenation, Green–Tao quantitative Leibman (with its erratum; Section 6.1 is titled 'The corrected quantitative equidistribution input'), Zorin-Kranich nilpotent IP recurrence. Reliance on corrected/revised versions of deep inputs and on new 'lifting of face symmetries' arguments (Props 6.3, 7.5) are the places an expert would check first.
164.lean: none — no lean/docs entry and no comparator challenge for family 164.
164.summary: Proves Hindman's finite sums and products conjecture: every finite coloring of the positive integers contains sets of any prescribed finite size whose nonempty subset sums and nonempty subset products all have one common color.

papers.title: Monochromatic finite sums and products in the positive integers

165.explainer: Crossing numbers of complete graphs are the canonical hard problem of topological graph theory: the conjectured formulas come from explicit drawings and only exact small cases and ~98% asymptotic lower bounds were known. The new lower-bound idea is algebraic: signed crossing counts plus the cyclic edge order at each vertex form a bilinear form that vanishes on every pair of cycles; weighting cycles by Lagrange-interpolation polynomials turns this into (i) an injective evaluation map from a polynomial space of dimension C(s,2)^2 into coordinates indexed by crossing edge pairs, and (ii) total isotropy of its image under a nondegenerate form, so the number of crossing pairs is at least twice that dimension. For K_{m,n} the same pairing feeds a subspace-intersection inequality on ranks of matrix differences.
165.caveats: Astonishingly short (13 + 16 pages) for two problems open 60-80 years; the proofs are algebraic (Tutte-style signed-intersection cycle pairing + polynomial interpolation + a totally isotropic subspace dimension count / subspace-intersection inequality), not computer searches, and the K_n paper explicitly does not depend on the K_{m,n} formula but borrows the cycle-pairing lemma and normalization appendix from it. Applies to ordinary crossing number (point count); pair/odd crossing numbers not addressed.
165.lean: main theorem formalized — CompleteCrossing.lean: OAI.Paper170.complete_graph_crossing_number (line 81), cr(K_n) = hill n for n >= 3; BipartiteCrossing.lean: OAI.Zarankiewicz.mainTarget_proof (line 60.
165.summary: Resolves the Harary–Hill conjecture and Turán's brickyard problem in the Zarankiewicz formulation, determining the crossing numbers of every complete and complete bipartite graph. The result proves the optimality of the classical drawings among all plane drawings with continuous edge arcs.

papers.title: The crossing number of complete graphs
The crossing number of complete bipartite graphs

166.explainer: Erdős asked how few distinct distances n points can span; in d dimensions the grid gives about n^{2/d}, and matching that lower bound was open (the 3D case reached n^{2/3−o(1)} only in August 2026). The proof follows the Elekes–Sharir/Guth–Katz idea: equal distances |p−p'| = |q−q'| become intersections of affine flats in a space of skew-symmetric matrices (rigid motions), and a polynomial-rank (Hilbert function) argument shows these flats cannot all be cut out by low-degree polynomials. The hard part is a multiscale argument ruling out the points concentrating on low-degree 'sparse cones', which is what lets the constant survive with no o(1) loss.
166.caveats: Unformalized, 103 pp of heavy real/complex algebraic geometry (Hilbert-function estimates, approximate complete intersections, multiscale 'sparse cones' argument), appearing ~6 weeks after the 147-page Tidor–Yu–Zakharov n^{2/3−o(1)} breakthrough for R^3 and leaning on its methods (flat geometry, degree-sensitive incidences); it claims both all d ≥ 3 and the exact constant-factor form, which even TYZ did not get in d=3. A prior constant-factor claim was withdrawn (per the paper). Highest risk in this batch along with 157's counterexamples.
166.lean: none — no lean/docs/166.md and no comparator challenge.
166.summary: For every fixed d ≥ 3, any n ≥ 2 distinct points in ℝᵈ determine at least c_dn^(2/d) distinct distances, with c_d > 0 depending only on dimension. This matches the integer-grid order and resolves the higher-dimensional Erdős distinct-distances conjecture with a constant-factor bound.

papers.title: The higher-dimensional Erdős distinct-distances conjecture

167.explainer: The unit distance problem asks how many pairs among n planar points can be exactly 1 apart: the answer lies between n^{1.014} (a 2026 AI-found number-field construction) and n^{4/3} (a 1984 incidence bound), and the second paper claims the 4/3 is not sharp. Both papers use the same new idea: after moving the configuration into a number field, write squared distance as (z−z')(w−w') with z = x+iy, w = x−iy, and use the product formula (logs of absolute values sum to zero across all places) to turn many repeated distances into contradictory height/entropy constraints. For pinned distances this shows that for almost every point, few of its distance classes can be large, so almost every point sees n^{1−ε} distinct distances.
167.caveats: Both results break long-standing barriers (Katz–Tardos 0.864 for pinned; 4/3 for unit distances, which is tight for unit circles in general normed/incidence settings, so any proof must use Euclidean arithmetic — here via the product formula over number fields after specialization, a plausible and genuinely new ingredient echoing the arithmetic flavour of the May 2026 disproof). Both are ineffective: no explicit β or rate; δ may be minuscule. Formalized, which is the strongest signal; still review 'unchecked'.
167.lean: main theorem formalized — both papers: OAI.WeakPinned.main, statement at lean/ComparatorChallenges/PinnedDistances.lean line 29 (∀ s > 0, F n s → 0; the pin-count corollary is a short deduction not itself in the challenge), solution OAI/Geometry/PinnedDistances/Main.lean, listed in formalization.yaml main_results.
167.summary: Proves the weak pinned Erdős distance conjecture: for every fixed ε > 0, all but o(n) points of any n-point planar set determine at least n^(1-ε) distinct nonzero distances. A complementary theorem bounds the number of unit-distance pairs by O(n^(4/3-δ)) for an absolute δ > 0.

papers.title: The weak pinned planar distance theorem
A power saving for planar unit distances

168.explainer: Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials encode intersection cohomology of Schubert varieties and are central to representation theory; the conjecture says the abstract shape of a Bruhat interval alone determines the polynomial, even though the definition uses group labels the poset forgets. The proof transports a reflection order from the second system to an edge schedule on the first, bounds how much each removed edge condition can grow the kernel modules of a moment-graph sheaf (via localization to rank-two dihedral pieces), and observes that the product of these bounds equals Dyer's path formula for the R-polynomial; reciprocity in both directions then forces every bound to be tight, giving equality of polynomials and closing an induction on interval rank.
168.caveats: The paper's proof uses moment-graph (Braden–MacPherson) sheaves and cites the Elias–Williamson character theorem / Fiebig's constructions as inputs, but comments inside the Lean development (Frobenius.lean, Decomposition.lean) state that the formalization does not prove BMP recognition or the Elias–Williamson character theorem, so the formal proof must follow a different/self-contained route than the paper's text suggests — worth expert scrutiny of how the formal and informal proofs relate.
168.lean: main theorem formalized — OAI.KLInvariance.combinatorial_invariance in lean/ComparatorChallenges/KLInvariance.lean (line 88); KL polynomials defined via Classical.epsilon on an explicit normalization (R-recursion, degree bound, reciprocity), with existence/uniqueness proved in the solution (CanonicalKL.lean…
168.summary: Resolves the full combinatorial invariance conjecture: isomorphic Bruhat intervals in arbitrary Coxeter systems have identical equal-parameter Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials. Thus the abstract order of the interval determines the polynomial, even across different Coxeter systems.

papers.title: Combinatorial invariance of Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials

169.explainer: Chromatic (quasi)symmetric functions record proper colorings; whether they expand positively in elementary symmetric functions was the Stanley–Stembridge problem, settled at q=1 in 2024, while the q-graded version (which also encodes the cohomology of Hessenberg varieties) stayed open. The paper identifies each graded e-coefficient with the Hilbert series of an algebraic object built in a quantum torus attached to the graph, proves positivity through filtrations and wall-crossing/mutation arguments, and then realizes the identities by finite bijections to assign each permitted permutation an elementary partition.
169.caveats: The q=1 case (Stanley–Stembridge) was already proved by Hikita in 2024, so this is the graded refinement plus an explicit permutation-indexed formula, not the classical conjecture — 'landmark' would overstate. The witness map theta is defined by a terminating procedure that may be very slow; it is not a closed-form rule. e-unimodality (other half of Shareshian–Wachs) untouched. Formal statement quantifies over finitely many variables r; equivalence to the symmetric-function identity is standard. No public expert reaction found.
169.lean: main theorem formalized — the comparator states it as data, not a Prop: def OAI.elementaryPositivityWitness (n) (G : NaturalUnitIntervalGraph n) : G.PermutationWitness in lean/ComparatorChallenges/ElementaryPositivity.lean (line 58).
169.summary: Resolves the elementary-positivity part of the Shareshian–Wachs conjecture: the chromatic quasisymmetric function of every natural unit interval graph has elementary-basis coefficients in ℕ[q]. The coefficients count explicitly described permutations, giving a combinatorial explanation of positivity.

papers.title: Elementary positivity of chromatic quasisymmetric functions

170.explainer: r(s,t) is the smallest n forcing either an s-clique or t independent vertices; since 1980 the upper bound t^{s-1}/(log t)^{s-2} was known, but lower-bound constructions were far off until Bradač (2026) matched the power of t, losing (log t)^{2s-4}. This work keeps the random ordered projective-flag graph (vertices = random point–hyperplane flags in PG(d,q), edges from one-sided incidence, so no d+1 clique) and proves sharply that long independent sequences are unlikely via an entropy-compression argument: a long consistent flag sequence would have a short description, contradicting its entropy lower bound. That shaves the log loss to the optimal s-2 up to o(1).
170.caveats: Builds directly on Bradač's 2026 construction (which already gave the right power of t), so the summary's 'determining the logarithmic exponent' is accurate but the conceptual leap (polynomial exponent) is Bradač's, not this release's. Does not touch r(4,t), where the log exponent is still between 2 and 4 (Mattheus–Verstraëte) — notable that the method needs projective dimension >= 4.
170.lean: main theorem formalized — Both papers: OAI.SharpRamseyFive.main in ComparatorChallenges/RamseyFive.lean line 25 (two-sided bounds with ε-dependent threshold and absolute C, plus the limit of (4 log t - log r(5,t))/log log t = 3), solution OAI.Combinatorics.RamseyFive.Main (450 files, ~60k lines).
170.summary: For every fixed integer s ≥ 5, proves r(s,t)=t^(s-1)/(log t)^(s-2+o(1)) as t → ∞, determining the logarithmic exponent and matching the classical upper bound at that scale. Here r(s,t) is the least number of vertices forcing an s-clique or a t-vertex independent set.

papers.title: The sharp logarithmic exponent of r(5,t)
Sharp logarithmic exponents for fixed off-diagonal Ramsey numbers

171.explainer: The hypercube Q_n has 2^n vertices but degree n, so standard results giving linear Ramsey numbers for bounded-degree or bounded-degeneracy graphs give constants that blow up with n; Burr and Erdős asked in 1975 whether cubes still have Ramsey number O(2^n). The proof assumes a red/blue colouring of C·2^n vertices with no monochromatic cube and shows each colour must then be almost perfectly pseudorandom (density 1/2 between all reasonably spread vertex distributions), using that any bias lets one embed a cube via common-neighbourhood sampling; then pseudorandomness itself is used to embed the cube by tiling it into subcubes and matching via Hall's theorem — a contradiction either way.
171.caveats: Unformalized single 172-page manuscript; a jump from exponent 2-c (Tikhomirov 2022) straight to linear is a very large step, so independent expert checking is essential. Proof is by contradiction on a counterexample sequence with N/2^n -> infinity at an unspecified rate, using a long chain of 'patch property' dichotomies (density gain vs discrepancy) over increasing width budgets, cluster exclusion, cube tilings in the style of Conlon–Fox–Lee–Sudakov, and a final Hall-type random two-element-subset embedding. Non-effective constant.
171.lean: none — no lean/docs entry and no comparator challenge for family 171.
171.summary: Resolves the Burr–Erdős hypercube Ramsey conjecture: the two-color Ramsey number of the n-dimensional cube is Θ(2ⁿ). Thus every red-blue coloring of a complete graph on a universal constant times the cube's number of vertices contains a monochromatic copy of the cube.

papers.title: The hypercube Ramsey number has linear order

172.explainer: Euclidean Ramsey theory asks which finite point sets cannot be avoided by any finite colouring of high-dimensional space; for 50 years the main question was whether 'spherical' or 'subset of a symmetric (transitive) set' is the right answer. The paper says the right answer is algebraic: A is Ramsey iff its sphere equation can be witnessed before multiplying out in the tensor square of its coordinate field. Necessity builds a colouring from a separating functional when no tensor exists; sufficiency turns the tensor into exact coordinate-permuted point lists at two scales and uses free-group paths, ultrafilters and Hales–Jewett to force a monochromatic copy.
172.caveats: The 'classification' is an algebraic tensor criterion over the coordinate field; deciding it for a given configuration is not obviously algorithmic (paper says it is not a procedure from numerical coordinates). The headline disproof of Graham's spherical conjecture is not new here (Pálvölgyi, arXiv:2609.23327, also AI-written); the new negative content is the LRW necessity disproof via Ramsey cyclic kites and the general criterion. The summary is accurate but understates that Graham's conjecture was simultaneously refuted.
172.lean: main theorem formalized — OAI.EuclideanRamsey.classification in lean/ComparatorChallenges/EuclideanRamsey.lean (line 42; hypotheses s>=2, d>=1, injective, full affine span; criterion stated with tensor product over Q of the coordinate IntermediateField), listed in formalization.yaml main_results.
172.summary: Classifies finite point configurations that occur monochromatically, at their original scale, in every finite coloring of sufficiently high-dimensional Euclidean space. The characterization is an algebraic condition over the coordinate field. It also disproves the Leader–Russell–Walters conjecture that every such configuration is a subset of a finite transitive set.

papers.title: A classification of finite Euclidean Ramsey configurations

173.explainer: In any network where friendship is one-way and never mutual, is there always someone with at least as many friends-of-friends as friends? The proof takes a minimal counterexample, deletes arcs to show every proper vertex set S has |F²(S) minus F(S)| below |F(S) minus S|, then blows each vertex up into a big transitive tournament to turn that into a strict set inequality. An extremal argument over pairs of 'compatible' families of vertex pairs, plus a new pruning lemma for arbitrary binary relations (proved via a matching bound and a rank argument), then contradicts that inequality.
173.caveats: Short (15 pp) for a 36-year-old problem, which cuts both ways: easy for experts to check, and the Lean statement is faithful and compact. The proof relies on Seacrest's subset perspective and the Brantner–Brockman–Kay–Snively product construction (cited, partly reproved in full). No public expert confirmation found as of 2026-10-07. Kingy.ai's survey notes the repository's own formalization status is 'unchecked'.
173.lean: main theorem formalized — OAI.SeymourSecondNeighborhood.exists_goodVertex, ComparatorChallenges/SeymourSecondNeighborhood.lean:34 (statement for any finite type with an irreflexive asymmetric relation; second neighbourhood defined as distance exactly two).
173.summary: Proves Seymour's second-neighborhood conjecture: every nonempty finite oriented graph has a vertex with at least as many vertices at directed distance exactly two as at directed distance one. Oriented graphs may be arbitrary apart from the exclusion of loops and oppositely directed edge pairs.

papers.title: A proof of Seymour’s second-neighborhood conjecture

174.explainer: A k-edge-connected graph contains about k/2 disjoint spanning trees, so on average a tree uses only a 2/k share of every cut, but one tree has to be good for every cut at once. The proof repeatedly halves the graph while keeping a large packing of disjoint spanning trees: an effective-resistance step (built on Anari–Oveis Gharan's locally connected hierarchies) finds a packing on low-resistance edges, and an MSS-style selection keeps half the edges while every cut roughly halves too. The losses multiply to a bounded constant, leaving one tree that is C/k-thin.
174.caveats: Existence proof uses the Marcus–Spielman–Srivastava theorem (via an isotropic-vector theorem proved in an appendix) and a fixed-point argument; the constant C is not made explicit. The ATSP application is now only of structural interest since constant-factor ATSP is known. Whether the Lean development faithfully formalizes the MSS input in full is worth checking (no sorry was found, so it must be proven inside the library).
174.lean: main theorem formalized — OAI.StrongThinTree.strongThinTree (ComparatorChallenges/StrongThinTree.lean:38) and OAI.AlgorithmicThinTrees.algorithmic_strong_thin_trees (AlgorithmicThinTrees.lean:191); solution OAI/Combinatorics/ThinTrees (~57k lines), no sorry; only StrongThinTree is in formalization.yaml main_results.
174.summary: Resolves the strong thin-tree conjecture constructively. Every finite loopless k-edge-connected multigraph on at least two vertices has a spanning tree containing at most a universal C/k fraction of the edges of every cut. Such a tree can be found deterministically in polynomial time, even with binary-encoded parallel-edge multiplicities.

papers.title: The strong thin tree conjecture
A polynomial-time construction of strong thin trees

175.explainer: Thresholds of random structures are bounded below by 'expectation thresholds': cheap certificates showing a property is unlikely. Talagrand asked whether fractional certificates can always be rounded to integral ones at a constant loss, and whether a likely family's few-fold unions cover all but a cheaply-certified set. The proofs use an orthogonal (Fourier-type) expansion to produce nonnegative weights and a signed product over a 32-row array that turns a union-cover failure into a lower bound on 16th powers of those weights, then a multi-scale selector estimate for the rounding.
175.caveats: Constants are astronomically large (2^75 unions; 25·512^4 loss) but universal, which is all the conjectures ask. The decomposition paper (Oct 5) depends on the discrete-convexity paper from the same release. The decomposition conjecture was posed only in Aug 2026, so it is a young problem; Talagrand's two conjectures are the substantial part. Very short papers (10–12 pp each) with formal proofs for two of them: a strong signal.
175.lean: main theorem formalized — two of three papers: OAI.TalagrandThreshold.talagrand_expectation_threshold_equivalence (ComparatorChallenges/TalagrandExpectationThreshold.lean:52, constant 25·512^4) and OAI.TalagrandDiscreteConvexity.talagrand_discrete_convexity (TalagrandDiscreteConvexity.lean:47, k = 2^75), both in…
175.summary: Proves that integral and fractional expectation thresholds differ by at most a universal factor, and resolves Talagrand's discrete-convexity conjecture. An application proves the Ascoli–He–Park–Talagrand graph-decomposition conjecture: every graph's edges split into a universally bounded number of fixed pieces, each with containment threshold at most a universal constant times the original graph's integral expectation threshold. The pieces' embeddings need not agree on shared vertices.

papers.title: Graph Decompositions at the Integral Expectation Threshold
Integral and fractional expectation thresholds are equivalent
Talagrand’s discrete-convexity conjecture

176.explainer: When does a random graph contain a copy of a large graph H? The obvious obstruction is a subgraph of H that is expected to appear fewer than once; Kahn and Kalai conjectured that this obstruction is right up to a single log factor. The proof nests subgraphs chosen by a ratio maximisation (Tran's spread links), keeps all extension histories in a tree, and runs Mossel et al.'s Bayesian resampling at every node with the same random edge set, so the logarithmic sampling cost is paid once.
176.caveats: Constant 2048·e^50 is enormous but universal. Proves the bound with log of edge count, slightly stronger than the original log n form. The proof states it does not use the same-release Talagrand comparison. No public expert reaction found.
176.lean: main theorem formalized — OAI.LeanBlast.SecondKahnKalai.secondKahnKalaiBounds, ComparatorChallenges/SecondKahnKalai.lean:65; solution OAI/Combinatorics/GraphThreshold (~13.5k lines), no sorry; listed in formalization.yaml.
176.summary: Proves the second Kahn–Kalai conjecture: for every finite simple graph H with h ≥ 1 edges and at most n vertices, its appearance threshold in G(n,p) is at most C p_E(n,H)(1+log₂ h), with universal C. Here p_E is the least density at which every subgraph of H has expected copy count at least 1/2.

papers.title: The second Kahn–Kalai conjecture

177.explainer: Coboundary expansion is the higher-dimensional version of graph expansion that underlies topological overlap and some quantum-code and PCP constructions. The complexes are coset complexes of a group of polynomial matrices over a finite field, cut down by congruence quotients modulo t^m; the local structure is fixed (so degrees are bounded) while the global size grows. A twin-building argument shows the infinite complex has no low homology, which, together with known cosystolic expansion, upgrades to coboundary expansion in every degree.
177.caveats: Relies heavily on the Oppenheim–Valentiner-Branth cosystolic expansion theorem for KMS coset complexes and on affine twin-building geometry; the new content is the cohomology vanishing for the congruence tower mod t^m over a large odd prime field. Constants not explicit. It is surprising that a full formalization of building-theoretic inputs exists; worth checking what is assumed via definitions.
177.lean: main theorem formalized — OAI.CoboundaryExpanders.main, ComparatorChallenges/CoboundaryExpanders.lean:91; solution OAI/Combinatorics/Coboundary (~22k lines), no sorry; not listed in formalization.yaml main_results.
177.summary: Constructs arbitrarily large finite d-dimensional simplicial complexes, for every d ≥ 3, with uniformly bounded vertex degrees and uniform 𝔽₂ coboundary expansion in every degree below d. Together with the known graph and two-dimensional cases, this establishes the existence of such expanders in every positive dimension.

papers.title: Bounded-degree coboundary expanders in every dimension

178.explainer: Ramanujan graphs are the best possible sparse expanders; random ones exist, but building one deterministically in every degree has only been possible in the bipartite case. The algorithm builds the graph by deterministic partial pairings and edge switches, choosing each step to keep resolvent and trace statistics on track (a derandomised random-graph process), and finishes with a local exact spectral repair that pushes the last eigenvalues strictly inside both edges of the Ramanujan interval.
178.caveats: Existence was already known from Huang–McKenzie–Yau; the new content is a deterministic polynomial-time construction (the exponent may depend on d, so not polynomial jointly in n and d, and not locally explicit/strongly explicit). Long (85 pp), delicate resolvent and trace estimates, no formalization: the least-checked result in this batch. Does not resolve the Bilu–Linial signing conjecture.
178.lean: none — no lean/docs entry or comparator challenge for family 178.
178.summary: For every fixed d ≥ 3, constructs a simple d-regular nonbipartite Ramanujan graph on every sufficiently large even number n of vertices, with every nonconstant adjacency eigenvalue strictly between -2√(d-1) and 2√(d-1). A deterministic algorithm outputs the full adjacency list in polynomial bit time, with exponent depending on d.

papers.title: Deterministic nonbipartite Ramanujan graphs in every fixed degree

179.explainer: A circulant Hadamard matrix is a ±1 sequence whose cyclic shifts are mutually orthogonal; Ryser conjectured only the trivial order 4 example exists, and the even case of Barker sequences (used in radar pulse compression) hinges on it. Classical arithmetic forces n = 4u^2 with u odd; the new step evaluates the sequence's group-ring element at characters on the 4-part and odd part, forms an alternating product of character values that must be a root of unity of odd order, and shows via a 2-adic residue computation that an identity of these products forces a nonzero alternating sum to vanish — impossible unless u = 1.
179.caveats: A 60-year-old problem with a long history of failed claimed proofs, settled in a 15-page paper — extraordinary, and the informal argument is dense algebraic number theory. The decisive credibility signal is the Lean formalization of the exact statement (if the build is sound, this is verified). The Barker corollary relies on classical external results for odd lengths (not formalized). No public expert reaction found as of 2026-10-07.
179.lean: main theorem formalized — OAI.CirculantHadamard.exists_iff_order_one_or_four in lean/ComparatorChallenges/CirculantHadamard.lean (line 24; real ±1 circulant H with H H^T = n I), listed in formalization.yaml main_results.
179.summary: Proves that real circulant Hadamard matrices exist exactly in orders 1 and 4, resolving the circulant Hadamard conjecture. Together with classical Barker-sequence results, this shows that binary sequences whose nontrivial aperiodic autocorrelations have magnitude at most 1 exist at lengths n > 1 exactly when n ∈ {2,3,4,5,7,11,13}.

papers.title: The circulant Hadamard conjecture

180.explainer: Barnette's conjecture is the last surviving piece of Tait's 1884 attempt to prove the four-colour theorem via Hamiltonian cycles. Dualise: the graph becomes a sphere triangulation with black/white faces, and a Hamiltonian cycle corresponds to splitting the vertices into two sets that each induce a tree. The proof assigns each black triangle one of its corners ('Tutte states'), builds a weighted exponential sum over pairs of disjoint states in which every pair whose edge set contains a cycle cancels in sign (a 'disk identity' pins the winding phase), then shows the sum is nonzero via positive circulations, so a good pair exists and yields the two trees.
180.caveats: Remarkably short (11 pp) for a 57-year-old conjecture, and an existence proof via a nonvanishing finite exponential sum (non-constructive; no polynomial algorithm claimed). The faithful, topologically defined Lean statement is the strongest evidence; the hard part to formalize is the passage from a topological plane drawing to combinatorial faces/dual triangulation, so checking that the library proves (not assumes) that step matters. No public expert confirmation found.
180.lean: main theorem formalized — OAI.Barnette.main, ComparatorChallenges/BarnetteHamiltonian.lean:48; planarity is defined topologically (injective continuous paths in R^2 with disjoint interiors), cubic, bipartite, 3-vertex-connected, and a genuine single Hamiltonian cycle.
180.summary: Proves that every finite simple cubic bipartite planar 3-vertex-connected graph has a Hamiltonian cycle, resolving Barnette's conjecture. Equivalently, every three-edge path in a finite simple cubic 3-vertex-connected bipartite Pfaffian graph lies in a Hamiltonian cycle.

papers.title: Paired states and Hamiltonian cycles in cubic bipartite planar graphs

181.explainer: Can every graph's edges be split into linearly many cycles and leftover single edges? The previous best lost a log* n factor because the decomposition paid the full graph order at every one of the many density scales. This proof picks one scale layer whose expanding pieces are large enough to pay for a whole prefix of scales, identifies pairs of low-degree vertices to shrink the graph, solves the quotient by induction, and lifts each quotient cycle back to a real cycle by routing through reserved edges in the expanding piece.
181.caveats: C is not explicit. Builds directly on Bucić–Montgomery's expansion/path-closing method plus Lovász's path-cycle decomposition and the Aharoni–Haxell matching theorem; the new step is a multi-scale induction that charges work to one expanding layer and saves vertices by pair identification. erdosproblems.com could not be fetched (403); search snippets still list #184 as open. No expert reaction found.
181.lean: main theorem formalized — OAI.ErdosGallai.erdos_gallai, ComparatorChallenges/CycleDecomposition.lean:31 (∃ C > 0, ∀ n, ∀ G on Fin n, a decomposition into k <= C·n cycles/edges); solution OAI/Combinatorics/CycleDecomposition (~43k lines), no sorry; listed in formalization.yaml.
181.summary: Proves that the edges of every finite simple undirected graph on n vertices can be partitioned into at most Cn simple cycles and single edges, for an absolute constant C. This resolves the Erdős–Gallai cycle-decomposition conjecture, bounding the number of pieces linearly even for dense graphs.

papers.title: A linear cycle-and-edge decomposition of every graph

182.explainer: How large can a subset of {1..N} be if no two elements differ by a perfect square? It is known to be o(N) and at least N^{0.75}, but the best upper bound saved only exp(-sqrt(log N)), and Green and Sawhney asked for a genuine power saving N^{1-c}. The proof keeps only the 'major-arc' rational Fourier coefficients of the set, builds a nonnegative multilinear quantity (a d-th power seminorm from a reflection-positive finite-field probability law, chessboard-style) that dominates a power of the density, and shows it contracts by a power of N when passing to shorter square-step progressions; iterating the contraction gives the power saving.
182.caveats: The square-case power saving (the famous question) is reported as fully formalized, which is strong evidence; the general intersective and prime-argument papers (dated Oct 5, 2026, i.e. later) are unformalized. The prime-argument paper is explicitly conditional on another claim in the same release — 'The Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis: a zero-free half-plane Re(s) > 7/8' for all Dirichlet L-functions (its Theorem 5.1 input [16]).
182.lean: partial formalization — Only the square case: OAI.SquareDifference.power_saving in ComparatorChallenges/SquareDifference.lean line 10 (∃ c>0, C, ∀ N ≥ 1, ∀ A ⊆ [1,N], square-difference-free → |A| ≤ C N^{1-c}).
182.summary: For every fixed intersective integer polynomial h of degree k ≥ 2 with positive leading coefficient, proves that a subset of {1,…,N} avoiding nonzero values h(1),h(2),… as differences has size O_h(N^(1-cₖ)), with cₖ > 0 depending only on degree. Here intersective means having a root modulo every modulus. For prime arguments, a power saving also holds when h has a unit root modulo every modulus, with exponent allowed to depend on h.

papers.title: A power saving for intersective polynomial differences with an exponent depending only on the degree
A Power Saving for Polynomial Differences at Prime Arguments
A power saving for square-difference-free sets

183.explainer: How many lines through two of n points split the rest exactly in half? Since 1998 the best bound was Dey's n^{4/3}, from the crossing lemma applied to convex chains, while constructions only reach about n·e^{sqrt(log n)}. The paper shows the crossing-lemma packing bound cannot be tight: if it were, a limiting measure argument (rank coordinates from the slope sweep, three transverse foliations forcing Euclidean rigidity, a spatial measure of dimension >7/4) yields a contradiction, giving a little-o gain at a fixed scale which a recurrence turns into a power saving n^{4/3-eps}.
183.caveats: Exponent saving eps and constants are completely ineffective (limiting-measure/compactness argument), so the improvement is qualitative. The summary's k-set statement O(n(k+1)^{1/3-eps0}) rests on a shallow-cutting reduction in Sec 8.1 that is not in the Lean statement. Restricted to straight lines/points (no pseudoline analogue claimed). Proof is single-author-model, 31 pp of real-analysis machinery (Radon–Nikodym, a.e. differentiability, three-foliation rigidity); Lean check of Thms 1.1–1.2 is the strongest evidence.
183.lean: main theorem formalized — OAI.PlanarHalving.power_bounds in lean/ComparatorChallenges/HalvingLines.lean (line 45) covers Thm 1.1 (halving pairs <= C n^{4/3-eps}) and Thm 1.2 (all-rank switch bound under the paper's genericity conditions).
183.summary: Improves the planar halving-line bound to O(n^(4/3-ε)) for sets with no three collinear and an absolute ε > 0. More generally, an n-point set with no three collinear has O(n(k+1)^(1/3-ε₀)) strictly separable k-subsets for 1 ≤ k ≤ n/2, with an absolute ε₀ > 0. The constants and positive exponents are nonquantitative.

papers.title: A power saving for planar halving lines

184.explainer: Excluding a fixed clique K_r should make graphs behave like triangle-free ones: independent sets of size n log d/d and colourings with Delta/log Delta colours, but for 45 years every argument for r>=4 lost a log log factor. The proof takes the maximiser of an entropy-like functional sum w_v(1-log w_v) minus edge mass, shows its triangle mass is O(edge mass) by repeatedly splitting vertices according to coupled random walks inside neighbourhoods (an entropy-increment argument), and once triangles are under control reads off a large independent set; the colouring paper runs a weighted semi-random nibble on the cover graph, which is still K_r-free, using the same local adjustment lemma.
184.caveats: Two famous conjectures at once; extraordinary. The independence half is Lean-checked (strong evidence, and the formal statement looks faithful). The coloring half is a separate 29-page paper dated Oct 5 2026, two days before release, with no formalization; it reuses machinery from the independence paper plus nibble/LLL and a Gavinsky–Lovett–Saks–Srinivasan-type concentration, and is the least-vetted part. Summary/title emphasize the coloring result while only the independence result is checked.
184.lean: partial formalization — only (b): OAI.CliqueFreeLog.logarithmic_independence_bound in lean/ComparatorChallenges/CliqueFreeLog.lean (line 11), statement faithful (K_r-free, r>=4, averageDegree>=2, c·n·log d/d <= indepNum).
184.summary: Proves the Alon–Krivelevich–Sudakov coloring conjecture in correspondence-coloring form: graphs avoiding any fixed subgraph F need O_F(Δ/logΔ) colors when their maximum degree Δ is sufficiently large. Also proves the Ajtai–Erdős–Komlós–Szemerédi independence conjecture: for fixed r ≥ 4, every n-vertex K_r-free graph of average degree d ≥ 2 has an independent set of size Ω_r(nlog d/d).

papers.title: Correspondence coloring graphs with a forbidden clique
A logarithmic independence bound for clique-free graphs

185.explainer: For finite matroids Edmonds' intersection theorem is classical; for infinite matroids the analogous statements were conjectured in growing generality. The paper builds, using an ultrafilter rank, a countable self-dual uniform matroid whose bases satisfy an ordinal inequality, then places copies along a doubly infinite path so that any attempt to cover the ground set by two independent sets must 'descend' forever in ordinal rank, which is impossible. Self-duality turns the covering failure into failure of packing/covering and hence of intersection.
185.caveats: Refutes only the unrestricted versions; Nash-Williams' original finitary conjecture (and the finitary/cofinitary-mixed setting, open beyond Joó's countable results) remain untouched, as the paper and summary correctly state. Construction uses a non-principal ultrafilter (Choice) and a nonconstructive maximal-extension argument; the matroids are 'wild'. Mathlib's Matroid matches the BDKPW axiom system, so the formal check is meaningful. No expert reaction found.
185.lean: main theorem formalized — OAI.InfiniteMatroidCounterexample.main in lean/ComparatorChallenges/InfiniteMatroid.lean (line 23) using Mathlib's (infinite) Matroid: countable infinite E, two self-dual matroids, no covering by two independents, and no packing/covering partition.
185.summary: Disproves the unrestricted infinite matroid intersection and packing/covering conjectures in ZFC, using two self-dual partitional matroids on a countably infinite ground set. The same examples answer Joó’s partitional-matroid question negatively. They are neither finitary nor cofinitary, so Nash-Williams’ original finitary conjecture remains outside the result.

papers.title: A Counterexample to the Infinite Matroid Packing/Covering Conjecture

186.explainer: Friedgut and Kalai showed in 1996 that symmetric monotone graph properties jump from unlikely to likely within an edge-probability window of 1/log n, and conjectured the optimal 1/(log n)^2. The new proof restricts to a random block B of about sqrt(n) vertices, freezing all edges outside B: permutations of B survive, which bounds each conditional influence, and a combinatorial fact (a graph with <= k^2/2 edges has a non-isolated vertex of degree <= k) converts control of conditional low Fourier degrees up to k into original degrees up to k^2/2, giving Var <= C·I/(log n)^2; integrating the Russo–Margulis derivative yields the width bound.
186.caveats: Remarkably short (10 pp graph paper) for a 30-year-old conjecture whose best prior proof (Bourgain–Kalai) was deep, but the graph statement is machine-checked with an explicit constant, which is strong evidence. Improvement over Bourgain–Kalai is only the removal of an arbitrarily small eta in the exponent (and uniformity in p/eps), so 'major' rather than landmark. Hypergraph extension is a 2-day-old unformalized companion. No specific reaction found; Kalai's own blog (2026-10-07) praises the release in general without addressing this item.
186.lean: partial formalization — graph case fully: OAI.Problem313.sharp_threshold_width in lean/ComparatorChallenges/SharpThreshold.lean (line 51), explicit constant 2^19, faithful to Thm 1.1 (quantile defined by sInf, natural log).
186.summary: Proves the Friedgut–Kalai threshold-width conjectures for graphs and fixed-uniformity hypergraphs. For fixed 0 < ε < 1/2, every nontrivial increasing relabeling-invariant property crosses from probability ε to 1-ε within width O((log n)⁻²) for graphs and O_r((log n)^(-r/(r-1))) for r-uniform hypergraphs, r ≥ 3. The hypergraph influence bound also applies to nonmonotone properties.

papers.title: A uniform influence bound for hypergraph properties
A Sharp Threshold Bound for Monotone Graph Properties

187.explainer: In the Maker–Breaker game on the infinite grid, every small polyomino was known to be either a winner or a loser except Snaky, open for about 40 years. The proof defines a 'valid claim' (cells Maker must own A, envelope T free of Breaker, height h) and a combination rule: if Maker plays p, the intersection of the children's envelopes becomes Maker's, so a single Breaker reply cannot spoil all continuations. Starting from the six immediate completions, 722 combined claims build up to one with A empty, a 251-cell envelope and height 21, which is a winning strategy from the empty board.
187.caveats: Essentially a finite certificate plus a soundness lemma; machine-checked, so high confidence, but the Lean policy type quantifies Breaker as an arbitrary sequence and requires legality only before the final move; worth a human check that the strategy is non-anticipating (Policy sees only current sets, so it is). Niche problem area; 84 pages mostly printed certificates. No external reaction found.
187.lean: main theorem formalized — OAI.SnakyPrototype.snaky_winning_strategy_21_with_legal_states in lean/ComparatorChallenges/SnakyTwentyOne.lean (line 45): an explicit policy on Z^2 that, against every legal Breaker sequence from the empty board, holds a Snaky after 21 Maker claims (finite-board 251-cell/17x17 restriction…
187.summary: Settles the Snaky achievement problem: Maker can force the six-cell Snaky shape within 21 of its own moves on the initially empty infinite square board. Maker moves first, each player claims one free cell per turn, and translations, rotations and reflections count as wins.

papers.title: Snaky in 21 Maker moves

188.explainer: Removing random triangles from K_n until none is left is the simplest random greedy packing; how many edges survive was known only up to n^{o(1)} factors. The proof stops the process when density is about n^{-1/2+eps}, then represents the remainder via random priorities on triangles and a recursive survival test, compares it with an independent branching model whose survival probability is Spencer's (1+2Dt)^{-1/2}, and controls the discrepancy (repeated triangles) by counting collision witnesses. The one- and two-edge survival probabilities give first and second moments, pinning the constant 1/(2 sqrt 2).
188.caveats: Lean statement appears faithful and covers the full theorem, which strongly supports correctness despite the delicate o(1/D) second-moment estimates. Only the triangle case of Joos–Kühn's conjecture; general F and arbitrary pseudorandom starting graphs open. No expert reaction found.
188.lean: main theorem formalized — OAI.SharpTerminalLeave.sharp_terminal_leave in lean/ComparatorChallenges/TriangleRemoval.lean (line 55): L2 convergence, convergence in probability and of normalized expectation to 1/(2 sqrt 2), with the process modelled as a PMF iterated C(n,2) steps (enough for termination).
188.summary: Starting from the complete graph on n vertices, repeatedly delete a uniformly chosen remaining triangle. The terminal edge count is asymptotic to n^(3/2)/(2√2), with mean-square convergence after normalization by n^(3/2). This proves the triangle case of the Joos–Kühn sharp-constant conjecture.

papers.title: The sharp terminal leave in random triangle removal

189.explainer: Take n-1 disjoint red cliques of size m-1 with blue between them: no red m-cycle and no blue n-clique, so R(C_m,K_n) > (m-1)(n-1); EFRS conjectured one more vertex always suffices when m >= n. A minimal counterexample graph (no m-cycle, independence number < n) must have strong neighbourhood expansion and a large clique; for cliques of size >= 9, optimizing systems of paths between clique vertices yields too many independent vertices, and the remaining small-clique cases are finitely many path 'patterns' killed by an exhaustive computer search (also checked in Lean).
189.caveats: Since Keevash–Long–Skokan already settled all but finitely many pairs (non-effectively), this is a completion of a nearly-solved conjecture rather than a breakthrough, though making it exact for all small cases was the hard residual and the argument is self-contained (does not use the KLS constant). Computer-assisted: 3,099 pattern instances; the Lean development contains ~200 MB of generated certificates, so kernel checking is the real verification — attractive if it builds, but heavy. No public expert reaction found.
189.lean: main theorem formalized — OAI.CycleClique.thm_main in ComparatorChallenges/CycleCliqueRamsey.lean line 23 (for all m ≥ n ≥ 3, (m,n) ≠ (3,3): R = (m-1)(n-1)+1, and R(3,3)=6, with R defined via cycleGraph m ⊑ G or K_n ⊑ Gᶜ).
189.summary: Proves the Erdős–Faudree–Rousseau–Schelp conjecture: R(Cₘ,Kₙ)=(m-1)(n-1)+1 for every m ≥ n ≥ 3, except R(C₃,K₃)=6. This is the exact threshold forcing a red m-cycle or a blue n-clique in every red–blue coloring of a complete graph.

papers.title: Cycle--clique Ramsey numbers

190.explainer: Removal lemmas say that a matrix far from avoiding a pattern must contain many copies; property testers rely on the quantitative dependence, and polynomial dependence was conjectured for ordered binary matrices. The construction indexes rows and columns by a binary tree; a 64x64 'anchor' block forces any pattern copy into prescribed roles, and the 2x2 core [[1,0],[1,1]] makes avoidance propagate a 1 and a 0 down tree paths until they collide at the leaves, so every repair needs many edits, while genuine copies must use rare diagonal leaf cells, making the copy density superpolynomially small in eps.
190.caveats: Counterexample is for one explicit large pattern; whether small patterns admit polynomial removal is open. The 'conjecture' was posed as a problem/question (Alon–Ben-Eliezer Problem 1.4; Gishboliner–Shapira survey conjecture), so 'disproves conjecture' is accurate but the problem is specialist. Formal check is complete and faithful.
190.lean: main theorem formalized — OAI.Problem348.no_polynomial_removal_bound in lean/ComparatorChallenges/MatrixRemoval.lean (line 63) with the explicit fixedH 66x66 pattern; for all c,C>0 exists n, eps, A with distance >= eps and copyCount < c eps^C n^132.
190.summary: Disproves polynomial ordered binary matrix removal with one fixed 66×66 zero–one pattern. Matrices can require many binary-entry changes to become pattern-free while their copy density is smaller than every proposed polynomial bound in that distance. Copies preserve row and column orders and match both zeros and ones.

papers.title: Polynomial removal fails for ordered binary matrices

191.explainer: Heilbronn asked how large the smallest triangle among n points in a unit square can be forced to be; for 40 years the best construction beat the trivial n^{-2} only by log n. The construction picks points (u1/u3, u2/u3) from integer columns whose labels lie on a finite-field parabola, encodes the field norm as a determinant coefficient via base-B digits so that distinct labels force a nonzero (not small) determinant, adds a second congruence condition on a quadric to rule out collinear triples, and then deletes the rare bad triples, yielding a power saving n^{eta}.
191.caveats: First rigorous polynomial improvement over the 1982 KPS log n factor, if correct; Lean check makes this very credible. The exponent is absurdly small, so quantitatively negligible; the gap to the n^{-7/6} upper bound remains vast. Calling n^{-2+eps} 'the conjectured upper bound' overstates its status slightly (it is a folklore formulation, Erdős #507 just asks to estimate). Interpolation to all n is paper-only.
191.lean: partial formalization — OAI.Problem355.heilbronn_power_lower_bound (line 51) and almost_n_minus_two_refuted (line 59) in lean/ComparatorChallenges/HeilbronnTriangle.lean: an unbounded sequence of n with point sets having all triangles >= n^{-2+eta}, explicit eta, and refutation of the eventual n^{-2+eta/2} upper bound.
191.summary: For every sufficiently large n, constructs n points in the unit square such that every triangle has area at least n^(-2+c) for one absolute c > 0. This disproves the conjectured almost-n⁻² upper bound in Heilbronn's triangle problem, which asks how large the smallest determined triangle can be.

papers.title: A power improvement in the Heilbronn triangle lower bound

192.explainer: For a Boolean function of degree d, how much can it correlate with the sum of its inputs? Majority on d bits gives about sqrt(d), and Gopalan–Servedio conjectured nothing beats this by more than a constant. The paper builds 'observations' of independent signs whose output cells have low polynomial degree because of cancellation, and amplifies the ratio of retained variance of the coordinate sum to the degree cost step by step (one score selects a leaf, and an exceptional tag predicts the sum with error < 1), so after enough steps a sign readout beats C sqrt(deg) for any C.
192.caveats: Non-quantitative: proof uses CLT-based finite averaging, so the dimension needed for a given C is uncontrolled; the true growth of max sum fhat(i) versus degree (between sqrt d and d) remains open. Fully formalized with a faithful statement. No expert reaction found.
192.lean: main theorem formalized — OAI.SquareRootDegree.main in lean/ComparatorChallenges/SquareRootDegree.lean (line 57): both the signed violation for every C>0 and unboundedness of the absolute ratio; solution OAI.Combinatorics.BooleanFunctions.Main (~3.6k lines), axioms propext/Quot.sound/Classical.choice.
192.summary: Disproves the proposed square-root bound relating a Boolean function's linear Fourier coefficients to its polynomial degree. For every C > 0, there is a sign-valued Boolean function f with ∑ᵢf̂({i}) > C√(deg (f)). Thus its total signed correlation with individual input bits can exceed the proposed bound by an arbitrary factor.

papers.title: Unbounded Violations of the Square-Root Degree Bound

193.explainer: Serre defined intersection multiplicity of two subvarieties of a regular scheme as an alternating sum of Tor lengths and conjectured it is positive when they meet properly. The remaining case was ramified mixed characteristic. The proof passes to perfectoid-type algebras where Koszul homology has normalized length zero, then uses rational K-theory with supports to show ordinary and normalized Euler characteristics agree after averaging over Galois conjugates, each of which is positive.
193.caveats: The Lean dir OAI/RingTheory/Multiplicity exists but no main_results entry for Serre; treat as unformalized. The proof combines perfectoid normalized-length methods (Cai–Lee–Ma–Schwede–Tucker), Faltings' normalized lengths, Bhatt–Scholze almost purity and Land–Tamme K-theoretic descent — heavy machinery, 31 pp. Prior AI-assisted claim (Editan, Dec 2025) on the same problem is a caution flag for the area.
193.summary: Proves strict positivity of Serre's intersection multiplicity χ^R(M,N) for nonzero finitely generated modules over any regular local ring, provided M⊗_R N has finite length and dim M+dim N=dim R. This resolves the positivity conjecture, including ramified mixed characteristic.

papers.title: Positivity of Serre's Intersection Multiplicity

194.explainer: Multiplicity measures how singular a local ring is; Lech conjectured it can't drop along a flat map. The proof works in characteristic p through Hilbert–Kunz and Dutta multiplicities and Cohen factorizations (Ma's framework), with reductions to all characteristics.
194.caveats: Lean (lean/docs/194.md): only a supporting characteristic-p comparison (Dutta multiplicity vs Hilbert–Samuel multiplicity over a complete domain; comparator DuttaDomain.lean) — not the theorem. 41 pp.
194.summary: Proves e(R) ≤ e(S) for every flat local homomorphism of nonzero Noetherian local rings, where e is Hilbert–Samuel multiplicity. This resolves Lech's conjecture in every dimension and characteristic.

papers.title: Lech's multiplicity conjecture

195.explainer: A small Cohen–Macaulay module would make a singular local ring look 'Cohen–Macaulay' via a finite module, and its existence would imply several homological conjectures. The counterexample shows no finite module can have full depth, via a numerical (Chern-character/slope) obstruction on a resolution of an explicit surface.
195.caveats: Characteristic 0 (contains C); the construction is a local ring of a branched cover of a blown-up plane surface cone with a Chern-character inequality obstruction (17 pp). The char-p and mixed-char versions are not addressed. No Lean.
195.summary: Constructs a three-dimensional complete Noetherian normal local domain over ℂ with no nonzero finitely generated maximal Cohen–Macaulay module. A three-dimensional local domain essentially of finite type over ℂ has the same property, disproving the domain form of the small Cohen–Macaulay module conjecture.

papers.title: A Complete Local Domain without a Small Cohen–Macaulay Module

196.explainer: Kaplansky asked whether the group algebra K[G] of a torsion-free group has no zero divisors. The construction immerses two finite graphs into a rose (free group), builds a graphical small-cancellation-type group where the coefficient counts of α·β cancel in pairs over F2 (parity), and separately proves torsion-freeness and asphericity by cone surgeries.
196.caveats: Lean: ComparatorChallenges/TorsionFreeZeroDivisors.lean states ∃ finitely presented torsion-free G with a finite 2-dim CW K(G,1) (Hausdorff, path-connected, contractible cover) and nonzero α, β ∈ MonoidAlgebra (ZMod 2) G with αβ = 0 — the full claim incl. the 'moreover'; proof OAI.TorsionFreeZeroDivisors.main at OAI/Algebra/GroupRing/Main.lean:13. Standard axioms; review 'unchecked'; I did not run the checker. Over F2 only (char 0 untouched). Implies (with known results) failure of unit conjecture variants for this group too.
196.summary: Constructs a finitely presented torsion-free group G whose group algebra 𝔽₂[G] has nonzero zero divisors, disproving Kaplansky's zero-divisor conjecture. The group has a finite two-dimensional classifying space.

papers.title: A Torsion-Free Group Algebra with Zero Divisors

197.explainer: Direct finiteness asks whether a one-sided inverse in a group algebra is two-sided (ab = 1 ⇒ ba = 1); it holds in characteristic 0 and for all sofic groups. A counterexample therefore produces the first provably non-sofic group, also refuting Gottschalk's surjunctivity (an injective cellular automaton that is not surjective). The construction reuses the zero-divisor graph-and-cone machinery to force cancellation patterns that a one-sided inverse needs.
197.caveats: Lean formalizes the TORSION versions only: KaplanskyFinitelyPresented.lean (finite char-2 field, finitely presented group with an element of odd prime order; OAI/RingTheory/DirectFiniteness/FinitelyPresented.lean:35), OddKaplansky.lean (OAI/Algebra/OddKaplansky/Main.lean:81), GroupRingDeterminant.lean (derived in Lean from the char-2 counterexample, OAI/Analysis/GroupDeterminants/Main.lean:13).
197.summary: Constructs a finitely presented torsion-free nonsofic group whose group algebra over 𝔽₂ is not directly finite, disproving Kaplansky's conjecture even without torsion. Companion examples give injective nonsurjective cellular automata on all configurations, refuting Gottschalk's surjunctivity conjecture. Another counterexample is an integral group-ring matrix, invertible over the rational group ring, with Fuglede–Kadison determinant strictly between zero and one, disproving the unrestricted Determinant Conjecture.

papers.title: A Torsion-Free Group Algebra That Is Not Directly Finite
A Counterexample to Kaplansky's Direct-Finiteness Conjecture in Characteristic Two
A Counterexample to the Group-Ring Determinant Conjecture
A Counterexample to Kaplansky's Direct-Finiteness Conjecture in Odd Characteristic

198.explainer: The finitistic dimension measures the longest finite projective resolution of a module; Bass conjectured it is finite for every finite-dimensional algebra, a statement known to imply the Nakayama conjecture. The counterexample is a fixed complex algebra built from tensor functors between two factors, carrying modules with arbitrarily long yet finite resolutions; Lean checks the projective-dimension bounds.
198.caveats: Lean: LittleFinitistic.lean (OAI.LittleFinitistic.Main.exists_counterexample at OAI/Algebra/Finitistic/Main.lean:44) and FinitisticAsymmetry.lean (OAI/Algebra/FinitisticAsymmetry/Main.lean:48); littleFinitisticDimension defined in the challenge via Mathlib's projectiveDimension — faithful. Review 'unchecked'. Consistent with family 199 (Nakayama counterexamples). 24 pp.
198.summary: Constructs a finite-dimensional complex algebra whose finite-dimensional modules have unbounded finite projective dimensions. This disproves the little finitistic-dimension conjecture.

papers.title: An algebra of infinite little finitistic dimension

199.explainer: These conjectures all say, in various forms, that a module with no self-extensions is projective (rigid ⇒ trivial). A symmetric algebra with a non-projective module having vanishing self-Ext in every positive degree is the cleanest violation; building the endomorphism algebra of A ⊕ M then turns it into a counterexample to the Nakayama conjecture (a minimal injective resolution of projectives but infinite injective dimension).
199.caveats: Lean: AuslanderReiten.lean (OAI.ArExplicit.Statement.main, OAI/Algebra/AuslanderReiten/All.lean:738, also records A/rad A ≅ k⁸, rad⁴ ≠ 0 and field-extension stability) and Tachikawa.lean (OAI.Tachikawa.main_theorem, OAI/RingTheory/Tachikawa/Counterexample.lean:293; k = FractionRing(MvPolynomial (Fin 3) (ZMod 2)), symmetric algebra via an explicit bilinear-form equivalence, Ext via Mathlib's CategoryTheory.Abelian.Ext). The Nakayama/Auslander–Gorenstein/Wakamatsu consequences via Γ_K are NOT formalized (lean/docs/199.md).
199.summary: Constructs finite-dimensional algebras over a characteristic-two rational-function field that disprove the Auslander–Reiten and Gorenstein-projective conjectures, and Tachikawa's second conjecture. An associated endomorphism algebra also disproves the classical, generalized and strong Nakayama conjectures, the Auslander–Gorenstein conjecture, and the Wakamatsu tilting conjecture. The counterexamples persist under every extension of the base field.

papers.title: An explicit counterexample to the Auslander-Reiten conjecture
A counterexample to Tachikawa's second conjecture

200.explainer: EGH predicts that among ideals containing a regular sequence of given degrees, the 'lex-plus-powers' ideal has the fewest possible generators in each degree growth — a Macaulay-type theorem for complete intersections with applications to Cayley–Bacharach. The Betti-number version is stronger.
200.caveats: Char 0 only (positive characteristic not claimed). Two independent proofs (Betti version 22 pp; Hilbert-function version 43 pp, the latter using a curve/fiber-product construction). No Lean.
200.summary: Proves the Eisenbud–Green–Harris and lex-plus-powers conjectures over every characteristic-zero field. Any homogeneous ideal containing a regular sequence, of arbitrary length and degrees at least two, admits a lex-plus-powers ideal with the same Hilbert function and no smaller graded Betti numbers.

papers.title: The Artinian Lex-Plus-Powers Betti Theorem
Commuting Division-Coefficient Forms and the Artinian Eisenbud--Green--Harris Conjecture

201.explainer: Kurosh asked whether a division ring all of whose elements are algebraic over the centre must be locally finite (finitely generated subrings finite-dimensional) — a Burnside-type question. The construction solves free-series equations step by step inside a central division algebra limit, keeping every element algebraic while generation by two elements forces infinite dimension.
201.caveats: Lean dir OAI/RingTheory/Kurosh exists but no main_results entry and no doc for 201 — treat as unformalized. The centre is not prescribed (construction over a countable central subfield plus finite descent). 45 pp.
201.summary: Constructs a countable characteristic-zero division ring that is algebraic over its center and generated by two elements over that center, but has infinite dimension over it. This answers Kurosh's division-ring problem on local finiteness negatively.

papers.title: A Counterexample to Kurosh’s Division-Ring Problem

202.explainer: Alperin's conjecture counts simple modular representations of a finite group locally: their number equals the number of 'weights' (defect-zero characters of p-local normalizers). The proof turns both sides into weighted counts of tuples solving a commutator-product equation, then shows the leftover terms vanish p-adically by realizing tuple counts as orbits on covers of a high-index genus-one curve in characteristic p.
202.caveats: RED FLAG for extra scrutiny (not error): the proof does NOT use the classification of finite simple groups or inductive conditions. It reduces the weight equality (via Knörr–Robinson chain inversion and central traces) to Theorem 3.1, a uniform p-power divisibility statement for counts of generating tuples (x,y,u1..un) with [x,y]u1⋯un = 1, proved by arithmetic geometry of marked genus-one curves of large index in characteristic p with inseparable genus estimates and valued-field descent.
202.summary: Proves the numerical blockwise Alperin weight conjecture for every prime and every finite group: the number of irreducible Brauer characters in a block equals the number of conjugacy classes of its weights.

papers.title: The Blockwise Alperin Weight Conjecture

203.explainer: Donovan's conjecture says that once the defect group is bounded, blocks of group algebras come in finitely many module-category types. It splits into bounding Cartan invariants and bounding Morita–Frobenius numbers; the paper bounds projective multiplicities uniformly over field size and rank for groups of Lie type, then handles group extensions by equivariant Frobenius comparisons.
203.caveats: Uses CFSG (reduces to quasisimple groups; Lie-type case via tilting objects on two-flag spaces after Eteve, Harish-Chandra moves for classical groups of unbounded rank). 116 pp across two papers. The proof's two controls are summarized in the paper's Figure 1. No Lean.
203.summary: Proves Donovan's conjecture: over each fixed algebraically closed field of characteristic p, blocks of finite groups with bounded defect-group order have only finitely many Morita-equivalence classes, for every prime p. Also proves the integral form over each fixed complete mixed-characteristic discrete valuation ring with algebraically closed residue field.

papers.title: Donovan's Conjecture over Algebraically Closed Fields
Integral Donovan Finiteness over Witt Vectors

204.explainer: Saturation says that if a tensor-product invariant appears after scaling all weights by N, it already appears unscaled — Knutson–Tao's honeycomb theorem in type A. The paper proves it for even spin groups via a deformation of 'half relations' on a graph of components.
204.caveats: Type D only (E6–E8 remain). 46 pp. No Lean (despite a RepresentationTheory/Tensor dir; no main result).
204.summary: Proves saturation factor one for Spin (2n), n ≥ 2: for three dominant integral weights whose sum lies in the root lattice, an invariant at any common positive integral dilation already gives an invariant at the original weights. This resolves the type-D part of the simply-laced saturation conjecture.

papers.title: Tensor saturation for even spin groups

205.explainer: Saxl conjectured that the staircase representation is 'universal': its tensor square contains every irreducible representation of the symmetric group. The proof exhibits, for each target, an explicit vector in a cyclic polytabloid submodule of the tensor square that generates a copy of it, extending Ikenmeyer's triangular tensor layers; Lean checks the positivity of all Kronecker coefficients.
205.caveats: Lean: Saxl.lean (OAI.Saxl.saxl_conjecture at OAI/RepresentationTheory/Saxl/Main.lean:88, via saxl_of_cyclic_support) and UniversalTensorSquares.lean; the stronger 'single cyclic tensor' claim is not included (lean/docs/205.md). The one `axiom` line found by grep in OAI/RepresentationTheory should be checked against the Saxl import closure (comparator would reject a non-standard axiom anyway).
205.summary: Proves Saxl's conjecture: the tensor square of every staircase representation contains every irreducible complex representation of the corresponding symmetric group. More generally, every Sₙ with n ∉ {2,4,9} has an irreducible representation whose tensor square contains all irreducibles.

papers.title: Universal Tensor Squares for Symmetric Groups
A Cyclic Polytabloid Proof of Saxl's Conjecture

206.explainer: Which finite lattices arise as the lattice of congruences of a finite algebra? Grätzer–Schmidt showed every lattice does if infinite algebras are allowed; for finite algebras the question is equivalent to asking which finite lattices are intervals in subgroup lattices of finite groups. The paper gives a graph-colouring characterization, finds a lattice failing it, and encodes undecidable problems into the criterion.
206.caveats: Lean (lean/docs/206.md): only the coloured-graph characterization equivalence (FiniteCongruenceGraph.lean) — the negative answer and undecidability are NOT formalized. Huge: 180 + 87 pp. The obstruction lattice is self-dual, also not an intermediate-field lattice of a finite separable extension. No public reaction found.
